#746. Paleontologists discover “one-in-a-million” fossil with 450-million-year-old soft tissue

A fossil dating back more than 450 million years has revealed something scientists almost never find: delicate soft tissues from an animal that lived hundreds of millions of years before dinosaurs appeared. The extraordinarily rare discovery is giving researchers a new understanding of how some of Earth's earliest marine animals lived, fed, and evolved.

The fossil belongs to an ancient crinoid, a marine animal related to modern starfish. Crinoids often resemble underwater flowers, with branching arms extending from a central body. More than 450 million years ago, these unusual creatures were among the animals thriving in Earth's earliest coral reefs, long before plants and animals had become widespread on land.

Although scientists have discovered millions of crinoid fossils, nearly all preserve only hard skeletal structures. Delicate body parts usually decay long before fossilization can occur, leaving major gaps in our understanding of how these ancient creatures functioned.

Now, paleontologists at the University of Oklahoma have identified an exceptionally rare specimen that preserves soft tissue structures, providing an extraordinary opportunity to investigate life in Earth's ancient oceans.

"After an animal dies, soft tissues like skin, eyes, or internal organs are the first things to decay," said Dr. Lena Cole, OU paleontologist and assistant curator of invertebrate paleontology at the Sam Noble Oklahoma Museum of Natural History. "Most fossils are only made up of hard parts like bones, teeth, or shells. Soft tissues are only preserved when the environment acts almost like a natural refrigerator or vacuum‑sealer -- conditions that are incredibly rare."

A 450 Million-Year-Old Fossil With Exceptionally Rare Soft Tissue

The remarkable specimen belongs to Dendrocrinus simcoensis, an extinct species of crinoid. Its preserved tube feet represent only the second known example of fossilized soft tissue in crinoids and the oldest such discovery ever documented.

Tube feet are small, flexible structures found in echinoderms, a group of marine animals that includes starfish, sea urchins, and crinoids. Because these structures are soft and easily destroyed after death, finding evidence of them in fossils is extraordinarily unusual.

"Preservation like this is truly one in a million," Cole added. "Crinoid fossils number in the millions, and this is only the second time soft tissues have ever been found."

The age of the specimen makes the discovery even more remarkable. These delicate structures have been preserved in the fossil record for nearly half a billion years, offering direct evidence of anatomy that would otherwise have disappeared.

"It's incredible these soft tissues have survived more than 450 million years," said Dr. David Wright, another OU paleontologist and assistant curator of invertebrate paleontology at the Sam Noble Oklahoma Museum of Natural History, who co‑authored the study with Cole. "For reference, these soft tissues are more than 200 million years older than the oldest dinosaur."

Ancient Feeding Structures Reveal Evolutionary Secrets

The fossil's preserved tube feet are especially valuable because they provide clues about how crinoids obtained food and interacted with their surroundings.

Unlike the teeth and jaws that many familiar animals use to eat, crinoids rely on specialized structures to capture food particles from seawater. Their tube feet play an important role in feeding and in how these animals interact with ocean currents.

The size, arrangement, and shape of these structures can differ between species, reflecting adaptations to particular habitats and feeding methods. By studying those differences, paleontologists can reconstruct aspects of an extinct animal's lifestyle, even when no living examples of that species exist.

"Since crinoid tube feet are used for feeding, you can think of them in a similar way to how we think about teeth in mammals," Wright explained. "Differences in their structure tell us about what kinds of environments a species lived in and how it fed."

Researchers also compared the ancient fossil with crinoids living in today's oceans. Those comparisons revealed notable anatomical differences, suggesting that the feeding structures of these animals have undergone substantial evolutionary changes over hundreds of millions of years.

"Comparisons with living crinoids show that the anatomy of this ancient species was very different," Cole added. "This gives us new insight into how crinoids evolved and how their feeding strategies changed over hundreds of millions of years."

A Rare Window Into Earth's Earliest Ocean Ecosystems

Beyond revealing details about one ancient species, the discovery could help scientists piece together how marine ecosystems developed during the early Paleozoic Era.

The Paleozoic was a vast chapter of Earth's history that began about 541 million years ago. During its early stages, marine environments supported an expanding variety of complex animals, while life on land was still relatively limited.

Crinoids were among the creatures that became established in early reef communities. Their fossils provide important evidence of how marine animals occupied different ecological roles and adapted to changing environmental conditions.

However, studying only living species cannot reveal the full range of forms and adaptations that existed in the distant past. Some extinct animals possessed anatomical features that have no close equivalent among their modern relatives.

"Fossilized remains of long‑extinct species can show features well outside the range of variation we see in living species," Wright said.

"By comparing ecological ways of life for extinct and modern species, we can understand how patterns of adaptive evolution have changed through time and what factors shaped the modern biosphere."

The biosphere includes all living organisms on Earth and the environments they inhabit. Understanding how it developed requires scientists to examine not only which species existed, but also how they interacted with their surroundings and one another.

Because soft tissues are so rarely preserved in ancient echinoderms, discoveries like this one provide evidence that conventional fossils cannot offer. They can help researchers identify previously unknown feeding strategies, understand ancient ecosystems, and trace evolutionary changes that eventually shaped modern marine life.

An Extraordinary Discovery Hidden in a Museum Collection

Perhaps one of the most surprising aspects of the discovery is where the fossil was found.

Although major paleontological breakthroughs are often associated with expeditions to remote locations, valuable scientific evidence can also remain unnoticed for decades in museums.

Fossil collections contain enormous numbers of specimens, many of which have never been examined by specialists with the expertise needed to recognize their most important features. As scientific knowledge and research methods improve, these collections can reveal discoveries that earlier generations overlooked.

"New fossil discoveries ultimately come from fieldwork, but museum collections play a significant role in this kind of integrative research," Wright said. "We don't always know the full significance of the specimens we collect. New technologies, ideas or expertise often find surprising ways to utilize existing specimens to make new discoveries."

The Dendrocrinus simcoensis fossil had been housed for years at Montréal's Musée de paléontologie et de l'évolution, a small museum that operates entirely with support from community donations.

Its remarkable scientific value became apparent when Cole and Wright, both specialists in crinoids, visited the museum and examined the specimen more closely.

Their investigation revealed that the fossil preserved an extraordinarily rare record of ancient soft tissue, transforming a specimen already held in a museum collection into an important source of new evolutionary evidence.

"This discovery highlights the importance of museum collections and the community support that keeps them alive," Cole said. "Without the dedication of many people caring for these collections, this research would never have been possible."

More Discoveries May Be Waiting in Museum Drawers

The finding also demonstrates why preserving and maintaining fossil collections is essential for future research.

At the Sam Noble Oklahoma Museum of Natural History, Cole and Wright oversee invertebrate paleontology collections containing more than one million specimens. Additional fossils are added every year, creating new opportunities to investigate ancient organisms and identify previously unrecognized species.

With collections of this size, no individual researcher could possibly examine every specimen in detail. A fossil that appears ordinary today might become the focus of a major discovery when studied by someone with a different specialty or new scientific tools.

Making collections available to researchers around the world increases the chances that these overlooked treasures will eventually receive the attention they deserve.

"This is why we work to make our collections accessible to researchers around the world," Wright said. "There are simply too many fossils to study over one person's career. There's more than a lifetime's worth of discoveries waiting to be found."

The extraordinary crinoid fossil is a reminder that some of the most revealing clues about Earth's distant past may already have been collected. They are simply waiting for someone to recognize what makes them special.

#745. The Chicks & Kacey Musgraves Complete Historic All-Female State Fayre 2027 Headline Bill

The country & roots-focused festival returns to Chelmsford, Essex, next summer.

The Chicks and Kacey Musgraves will join Shania Twain at the top of the bill for State Fayre 2027, completing an all-female headline lineup that organisers say is a first for a major U.K. camping festival.

Following its inaugural edition this summer, the festival heads back to Hylands Park in Chelmsford, Essex, between June 18-20. Twain was confirmed for the event in a post shared to State Fayre’s Instagram account on Nov. 2.

The Chicks, comprising Martie Maguire, Natalie Maines and Emily Strayer, will return to the U.K. for the first time since 2023, which included appearances at Glastonbury and BST Hyde Park supporting Bruce Springsteen. Musgraves will make her first festival headline appearance in the region, while Twain’s State Fayre slot forms part of a wider U.K. and Ireland summer run, which will see her perform in cities including Glasgow, Cardiff, Belfast and more through June 29.

State Fayre has also revealed its first wave of additional acts, with Billy Strings, Sam Barber, The Corrs, Drake Milligan, Sons Of The East, Brothers Osborne, Bear’s Den, Evan Honer, Noah James, Aaron Rowe, Mountain Grass Unit, Danny Worsnop, Taylor Acorn, Alyssa Bonagura and Bella McCormick among those confirmed. More artists are expected to be announced over the coming months.

Weekend and Saturday day tickets are available via the official State Fayre website. A presale for Friday and Sunday day tickets is now live via PayPal, ahead of general on-sale at 9 a.m (GMT) on Nov. 13.

In a press statement, State Fayre festival organisers Anna-Sophie Mertens and Alex Simmonds described The Chicks, Musgraves and Twain as “three incredible artists who each in their own way have inspired and represented vital change, within not only these genres but music as a whole.”

They continued: “To bring all three together as a U.K. festival first is something we’re very excited about. With further additions including in-demand Sam Barber, Billy Strings Brothers Osborne and The Corrs showing the breadth of what makes State Fayre what it is (and much more to be announced), we’re asking if it can be June 2027 already?”

Beyond the musical offerings, State Fayre will also bring experiential elements to the site including fairground rides and The Fume Pit, its dedicated barbecue area featuring more than 15 U.K. and international traders across the weekend.

Speaking to Billboard U.K. earlier this year, Mertens, who serves as senior vp of touring at Live Nation UK and sits on the Country Music Association’s board, discussed the festival’s ambition to bring different strands of country and roots music together under one banner.

“It’s really important for us to bring together a few different musical elements, but to ensure they blend together so that we could showcase the real depth of each genre,” she said. “There really isn’t any other event doing that at such a large scale.”

If NASA ever hopes to build a permanent moon base for astronauts, let alone aim for Mars, the U.S. space agency is going to need a whole lot of space travelers. And now, you have a chance to be one of them.

NASA on Saturday (Nov. 7) put out the call for a new class of astronaut candidates who think they have the "right stuff" to fly, live and work in space. Those astronaut hopefuls have until Dec. 3 to apply (the application website is here), with NASA planning to make its final selections in late 2027.

"This is an extraordinary time to join NASA's astronaut corps," the space agency's chief, Jared Isaacman, said in an announcement, which was made during NASA's "Max Power" air show at Kennedy Space Center (KSC) in Florida. "The people we select could walk on the moon, live and work at the Moon Base, and help pioneer the systems and operations that will ultimately carry crews to Mars."

It's been two years since NASA last sought applications for astronauts. In 2024, more than 8,000 people applied, though only 10 — five men and five women — made the cut. They're in the middle of a two-year training program right now.

This new 2027 astronaut group will be the 25th astronaut class in NASA history. Its announcement comes the same year that NASA returned astronauts to the moon for the first time since the Apollo era with the Artemis II moon flyby. Four more astronauts will test Artemis moon landers in Earth orbit on the Artemis III mission in 2027.

NASA currently has 32 active astronauts in its spaceflying corps. The agency has recruited 370 people to fly in space since 1959, when the first seven Mercury astronauts were selected and unveiled to the world.

"There is a lot to be done in order to get all of these new vehicles and the new suits and everything as we continue to work towards the moon, build a base there, stay permanently, and then eventually onto Mars," NASA astronaut Nichole Stilwell, class of 2021, told Space.com in an interview at KSC during the Max Power event. "And so we just don't have enough people, and we're looking for more."

If you're interested in applying to be a NASA astronaut, you should take a look at the requirements first.

NASA's core guidelines require applicants to be U.S. citizens and have a master's degree in a STEM field like "engineering, biological science, physical science, or computer science from an accredited institution," the space agency said in a statement. You'll also need at least three years of experience in your related field.

Don't have a master's degree? Here's three other ways NASA might consider your application, according to the agency's advisory:

If you're a medical doctor and are considering applying to be an astronaut, your residency training can be counted toward your professional experience, but only if it is completed by July 2027, NASA said.

If you want to be a pilot astronaut for NASA, you'll need some serious flight hours under your belt. Here's a rundown of some ways to meet that requirement:

"For those who apply, becoming a NASA astronaut is more than a career opportunity,” said NASA chief astronaut Scott Tingle, who also chairs the Astronaut Selection Board at the agency's Johnson Space Center (JSC) in Houston. "It is a chance to join a legacy of explorers who have pushed the boundaries of discovery and play a role in the missions that will shape humanity’s future in space."

Once NASA selects its 2027 astronaut class, the new recruits can expect to begin a two-year training program based out of JSC, which is home to the agency's astronaut corp and Mission Control.

“The window is open. The mission is waiting.," NASA Deputy Administrator Matt Anderson said in a statement. "And the only thing missing from the greatest adventure humanity has ever embarked upon is you."

Space.com Content Manager Chelsea Gohd contributed to this report from NASA's Max Power event at the Kennedy Space Center in Cape Canaveral, Florida.

#743. ‘The Body’ Review: Despite Modest Blessings, Netflix’s Catholic Schoolgirl Horror-Drama-Satire Leaves Much to Be Desired

Created by Quinn Shephard ('Under the Bridge'), the aughts-set series follows a group of teenagers who set off town-wide hysteria after a dance team initiation gone wrong.

The girls of St. Marks Catholic High School are no saints. They spend their weekends drinking and dancing and hooking up at parties; they spend their schooldays gossiping and lying and keeping secrets. At one point, they invoke Satan as a joke and then seal the pseudo-ritual by dropping molly, unwittingly kicking off a chain reaction of events that will threaten to swallow their town whole.

If only the sins committed by their show were nearly as exciting. While The Body is not without its modest pleasures, they’re spread too thin over eight hours gifted with more ambition than effectiveness. In its uneven mélange of two-dimensional characters and underexplored ideas, the Netflix drama does a finer job of paying tribute to its pop culture forebears than of staking its own claim among them. Related Stories TV Catholic School Dance Team Wreaks Havoc in First Trailer for Netflix's Raunchy Psychodrama 'The Body' TV Netflix Sets Premiere Date, Drops First Look for Raunchy Catholic School Psychodrama 'The Body' The Body The Bottom Line Neither heavenly nor hellish. Airdate: Wednesday, Nov. 11 (Netflix)Cast: Kristina Bogic, Geena Meszaros, Sara Boustany, Jackson Kelly, Nnamdi Asomugha, Sofia Wyle, Shirley Chen, Orlando Norman, Louisa Krause, Gabby WindeyCreator: Quinn Shephard

To TL;DR the premise, it’s Yellowjackets meets Carrie, at least to start. The tone is mostly straight-faced, neither bone-chillingly spooky nor bitingly funny, though it flirts from time to time with Emerald Fennell-ian excess and Ryan Murphy-esque irreverence, especially in the premiere directed by creator Quinn Shephard (Under the Bridge).

In the fall of 2004 — a setting you could carbon-date even without the caption by the velour tracksuits, Motorola flip phones and Balenciaga handbags, courtesy of costume designer Mirren Gordon-Crozier — the Lions, St. Marks’ all-female dance troupe, is holding tryouts. The team’s situation is dire: They’ve just lost a key member to injury in the weeks before regionals, and even the most promising of the new candidates, Grace (Sofia Wylie), is such a goody-two-shoes that co-captains Elise (Sara Boustany) and Anya (Kristina Bogic) disagree over whether she’ll be able to hang.

But the real trouble begins once a new girl is chosen for induction into the team. After a Halloween hazing ritual goes disastrously awry, the Lions are visited by strange visions and hard-to-explain occurrences that eventually blow up into a community-wide hysteria whose origins might be divine, demonic or just plain psychological.

Regardless of their true provenance, the show’s best weapon is its villain, who quickly makes herself known to us if not yet the characters around her. Lisbeth (Geena Meszaros) is a recent transfer whose painfully awkward affect and plain looks (achieved by bleaching a conventionally good-looking actor’s eyebrows into oblivion) make her an unlikely fit for this Lion’s den. Toss in that she lives in a shabby, Church-funded house with a strict fundamentalist mother, Catherine (Louisa Krause), and you might be tempted to take pity on her, as sweet Anya does when she impulsively invites Lisbeth to a party.

But having thus gotten her foot in the door with the cool girls, this kicked puppy quickly reveals herself to be a snake. Meszaros manages the impressive trick of making Lisbeth seem skin-crawlingly off-putting even when she’s not doing much at all — just chatting with Anya in her cloying singsong of a voice, or fluttering her fingers around a Bible like a child raring to go to town on a toy. Lisbeth is not a subtle or complex character, even if her psychology is broadly comprehensible (hurt people hurt people, and all that). But Meszaros makes Lisbeth’s one-dimensional coldness seem akin to an elemental force.

The other characters are saddled with similar flatness but, unfortunately, not the same compelling anti-charisma. It’s not for lack of effort on the part of the cast. Bogic and Boustany share a beguiling chemistry as thick-as-thieves besties who might be more if they could ever shake off the terror of being queer in a culture that considers it a grotesque perversion. Jackson Kelly gives a touching performance as Lisbeth’s little brother Leo, whose wide-eyed sincerity stands in marked contrast to the flagrant sinning and cruel carelessness that surrounds him. And while Gabby Windey, of The Traitors and The Bachelor fame, is essentially in a glorified cameo as the Lions’ indifferent and ineffectual coach Shauna, her kooky charm is welcome all the same.

It’s the writing that comes up short. Despite its luxurious run time, The Body struggles to flesh out its ensemble beyond their most basic narrative and thematic functions. The result is characters who are legible enough to understand, even for noncommittal second-screeners, but not quite interesting enough to love.

Missed opportunities abound. A storyline that pairs prickly Elise and pure-hearted Leo seems promising in its unpredictability, only for the dynamic to get dropped once it’s served its narrative purpose. Efforts to uncover the truth by Father Franklin (Nnamdi Asomugha) — the school priest, who also happens to be Grace’s uncle — provide dramatic tension but, strangely, precious little insight into how this whole ordeal might change a man of God’s relationship with his own faith.

Likewise, though The Body gestures at some interesting ideas, it lacks the curiosity, the courage or perhaps the capability to follow them into truly daring territory. The show’s aesthetic frequently plays in the blurred line between religious iconography and sexual imagery — as highlighted crassly in the “slutty angel” and “slutty God” Halloween costumes donned by the girls, and more loftily in classical paintings of tastefully nude saints in the throes of (supposedly spiritual) ecstasy. But it stops shy of taking that connection into darker or twistier or more surprising places. It’s content just to point out it exists.

The show suggests halfheartedly that the seeds of our present can be found in this era, in which characters watching TV flip between the sexualized vapidity of The Simple Life and the jingoistic violence of the Iraq War. (Donald Trump even makes a brief appearance, as host of The Apprentice.) But the references are too vague and too far between to amount to much more than a “Hey, remember this?” One gets the sense that the time period was chosen primarily for its trendy nostalgic appeal — which would be fine, except that as with so many of its choices, The Body seems to want it to be deeper than it is.

Which is fitting, in its way: What is religion if not a promise that you can be something more than you are, that something more profound awaits, that everything means something no matter how trivial or random it might seem at first glance? But if it’s transcendence you’re after, you’re probably better off seeking it in the pews. The Body, in its minor blessings and disappointing shortcomings, remains stubbornly of our own mundane world.

#742. A quantum breakthrough makes light behave like both a solid and a liquid

Scientists have demonstrated an extraordinary form of quantum matter that combines two properties that seem incompatible. Known as a supersolid, this unusual state has the orderly structure of a crystal while also displaying the frictionless flow associated with a special kind of liquid. Even more remarkably, researchers have now observed this behavior at room temperature, eliminating the need for the extreme cooling traditionally used to investigate such phenomena.

The breakthrough was achieved by an international team from the Faculty of Physics at the University of Warsaw, the Military University of Technology (Poland), IBM Research Zurich, and the French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS). Rather than relying on atoms cooled to temperatures near absolute zero, the scientists created a supersolid using particles that combine properties of light and matter.

Published in Science Advances, the findings introduce a new way to investigate exotic quantum behavior under much more accessible conditions. They could also help advance future technologies ranging from optical computing to highly sensitive sensors.

How Can Matter Behave Like Both a Solid and a Liquid?

Under ordinary circumstances, solids and liquids behave very differently. Crystals have an organized internal structure, with their particles arranged in repeating patterns. Liquids, by comparison, can flow and change shape.

Quantum physics, however, allows matter to behave in ways that would be impossible under the familiar rules of everyday life.

One example is superfluidity, a remarkable phenomenon in which a fluid loses its viscosity, or internal resistance to flowing. A superfluid can move through extremely narrow passages without experiencing the usual friction. Imagine placing an oar into such a liquid. You would encounter almost no resistance until the oar reached a certain speed. Beyond that threshold, tiny swirling structures known as quantum vortices would suddenly form.

During the 1960s, physicists proposed an even stranger possibility. What if a superfluid could also develop the repeating internal structure normally associated with a crystal?

This hypothetical combination became known as a supersolid. In such a state, the material exhibits the spatial organization of a solid while retaining the remarkable flow properties of a superfluid.

For decades, supersolidity remained a theoretical concept. Experimental confirmation finally arrived in 2017, when researchers observed the phenomenon in ultracold atomic Bose-Einstein condensates. These condensates form when particles enter a collective quantum state and begin behaving as a coordinated system rather than as separate individuals.

The catch was that producing these conditions generally required sophisticated equipment capable of cooling matter to temperatures extremely close to absolute zero, the lowest possible temperature.

Creating a Quantum Supersolid Using Light Instead of Cold Atoms

The international TopoLight consortium approached the challenge from a different direction. Instead of using ultracold atoms, the researchers worked with unusual hybrid particles called exciton polaritons.

These quasiparticles arise when light interacts so strongly with matter that the two become coupled inside a tiny optical chamber called a microcavity. The resulting particles display characteristics of both light and matter.

Exciton polaritons are extremely short-lived, typically surviving for only a few picoseconds. A picosecond is one trillionth of a second. Despite their brief existence, these particles can organize into a Bose-Einstein condensate and collectively exhibit the behavior of a quantum superfluid.

To create the necessary conditions, the team constructed an optical microcavity containing a specially engineered liquid crystal and covered it with an organic semiconductor. The arrangement allowed light and matter to interact strongly enough to produce the desired quantum effects without the need for extreme cooling.

"Our liquid-crystal microcavities can operate even at temperatures approaching 60°C," says Professor Wiktor Piecek from the Military University of Technology, whose group developed the liquid-crystal structures.

That temperature is approximately 140°F, far above the freezing conditions normally associated with experiments involving exotic quantum matter.

Strange Patterns of Light Reveal a Supersolid

How can researchers determine whether a collection of particles has entered such an unusual state?

In this experiment, the evidence appeared in the light emitted by the sample. When the system transitioned into the supersolid phase, researchers observed a series of regularly spaced bright fringes.

These patterns indicated that the particle condensate had spontaneously developed a repeating variation in its density. This type of spatial organization is a defining feature of crystalline structures and an important sign of supersolidity.

But the researchers noticed another intriguing effect.

Each time a laser pulse excited the sample, the bright fringes appeared in a different position. Rather than following a single fixed arrangement, the quantum system repeatedly selected among several equally possible configurations.

"This is a textbook example of spontaneous symmetry breaking," explains Professor Guillaume Malpuech from Institut Pascal (CNRS). "Theory predicted that the supersolid could choose among several equivalent states, and that is exactly what we observed."

Spontaneous symmetry breaking occurs when a system that could exist in several equivalent arrangements settles into one particular configuration. In this case, the effect became visible through the changing positions of the light patterns.

The condensate also displayed another unusual characteristic called a persistent spin helix. This refers to a repeating variation in the polarization of the emitted light. Polarization describes the orientation of light's oscillating electric field.

Together, these observations revealed two different forms of order occurring at the same time. One appeared in the intensity of the emitted light, while the other appeared in its polarization.

A Difficult Experiment With Only Hours to Succeed

Achieving these results required overcoming an unexpected practical obstacle.

The organic semiconductor used in the device gradually reacted with the liquid crystal. As a result, the experimental samples had a limited useful lifetime, giving the scientists only a few hours to collect their measurements after assembly.

This restriction made careful preparation essential. The researchers needed to determine exactly which measurements to perform and in what order before beginning each experimental run.

"We had to plan the entire sequence of experiments in advance," recalls Dr. Marcin Muszyński, the paper's first author, now a postdoctoral researcher at The City College of New York. "Repeating a measurement meant fabricating an entirely new sample."

The most important measurements took place at IBM Research Zurich. There, scientists deposited thin layers of the organic semiconductor onto specialized structures designed to manipulate light. These photonic structures had been manufactured at the Military University of Technology.

The semiconductor itself was not new to the researchers. IBM scientists had investigated its quantum properties for years, including its ability to support Bose-Einstein condensation.

"We have studied the organic semiconductor MeLPPP (methyl-substituted ladder-type poly(paraphenylene) for many years and previously observed Bose-Einstein condensation in this material," says Thilo Stöferle from IBM Research. "This was the first time we combined it with a liquid-crystal microcavity."

Bringing these materials together ultimately made it possible to observe the unusual supersolid behavior at room temperature.

Why Room Temperature Quantum Matter Matters

The significance of the discovery extends beyond demonstrating another unusual phenomenon predicted by quantum physics.

Many experiments involving exotic quantum states depend on costly cryogenic systems designed to maintain temperatures close to absolute zero. These demanding conditions make research more complicated and can create substantial obstacles when scientists attempt to turn laboratory discoveries into useful technologies.

The new results show that certain exotic quantum effects can instead be investigated in photonic devices that operate at ordinary temperatures.

This could create opportunities for future technologies that use light to process information. Potential applications include ultrafast photonic devices, specialized computing accelerators inspired by the way biological brains process information, and advanced optical sensors.

The computing approach, known as neuromorphic computing, seeks to imitate aspects of the brain's information processing to perform certain tasks more efficiently. Light-based systems could eventually provide new ways to accelerate these operations.

The supersolid's exceptional sensitivity to light polarization may also prove useful for developing sensors capable of detecting extremely subtle optical changes.

These applications remain possibilities for future research, but the ability to generate the underlying quantum behavior without extreme cooling represents an important step toward making such technologies more practical.

Electrically Controlled Quantum Matter Opens New Possibilities

One of the most promising features of the experiment is that the optical device can be adjusted using electricity.

The liquid crystal microcavities provide the first electrically tunable platform for studying supersolid exciton-polariton condensates. This means researchers can alter the optical properties of the system by applying an external voltage.

Earlier experimental approaches did not offer this same degree of electrical control.

The ability to adjust the system dynamically gives physicists greater flexibility when investigating how quantum states emerge, interact, and respond to changing conditions.

It could also become valuable when designing practical quantum photonic devices, where precise control over the behavior of light and matter is essential.

By combining room-temperature operation with electrical tunability, the researchers have established a versatile platform for exploring quantum phenomena that previously required far more demanding experimental conditions.

About the University of Warsaw Faculty of Physics

The University of Warsaw has a long history of research and education in physics and astronomy. Both disciplines became part of the university in 1816, when they were included in the Faculty of Philosophy. The university subsequently established its Astronomical Observatory in 1825.

Today, the Faculty of Physics includes the Institutes of Experimental Physics, Theoretical Physics, and Geophysics, along with the Department of Mathematical Methods in Physics.

Its research encompasses nearly every major area of modern physics, from the behavior of particles at quantum scales to the structure and evolution of the universe.

The faculty employs more than 250 academic teachers and serves approximately 1,350 students and more than 150 doctoral students.

According to Shanghai's Global Ranking of Academic Subjects, the University of Warsaw ranks among the world's top 150 institutions for physics education.

#741. Sade Won’t Be Attending the Rock Hall Induction Ceremony

"Please know that our absence takes nothing away from how much this recognition means to us," reads a statement from Sade.

It’s official: Sade won’t be on hand this weekend for their induction into the Rock And Roll Hall of Fame.

The elusive British act, fronted by the iconic singer Sade Adu, confirmed what should come as a surprise to none of their superfans, by way of a post on the band’s official website.

“Sorry we can’t be there in person to celebrate with the other artists,” reads the statement from Adu. “Please know that our absence takes nothing away from how much this recognition means to us.” Related Hilary Duff Reflects On Her Massive Lucky Me Tour: 'I'm Really Proud of Myself, and That's Hard to Feel As An Adult' The Chicks & Kacey Musgraves Complete Historic All-Female State Fayre 2027 Headline Bill Dua Lipa, Tame Impala & SZA to Headline Coachella 2027 Explore Sade See latest videos, charts and news

Adu is tapped for Rock Hall induction in the performer category along with bandmates Paul Spencer Denman (bass guitar), Andrew Hale (keyboards) and Stuart Matthewman (saxophone). Sade will be inducted after their second nomination (the first came in 2024), in a Class of 2026 that’s stacked with countrymen and women, from Phil Collins to Billy Idol, Iron Maiden, Joy Division/New Order and Oasis

“Being inducted into the Rock And Roll Hall of Fame is both a gift and a timely reminder to give thanks,” Sade’s message continues, “not only to those who voted for us but also every single person who lets our music into their lives.”

The band also paid tribute to Australian artist manager Roger Davies, and the late record producer Mike Pela, who died in 2022, aged 72. ”We are indebted to the ones who’ve been with us on this road to get here,” the Sade message reads. “Sade, Stuart, Andrew and Paul. Mike Pela, the fifth Sade…this is as much yours as ours Mike. Forever our soul mate.”

Formed in London in the early 1980, Sade, all class and groove, slid into the airwaves with several of the era’s creamiest hits, including “Smooth Operator” and “Sweetest Taboo,” which both peaked at No. 5 on the Billboard Hot 100 in 1985. Make no mistake, Sade was a leading figure in the second British invasion, only the group went to the top without the shoulder pads, teased hair or tabloid headlines.

Adu and her band have earned the reputation as one of the most enigmatic acts in music, with impressive gaps between albums. Sade’s most recent album, Soldier of Love, dropped in 2010, a full decade after its predecessor, Lovers Rock.

Across the group’s recording career, Sade has collected four Grammy Awards, including best new artist in 1986, topped the Billboard 200 with two titles (1985’s sophomore album Promise and Soldier Of Love), and its singer has received several royal honors for services to music, including an OBE in 2002, and a CBE in the 2017 Birthday Honours.

Sade joins Oasis on the sidelines of the Rock Hall’s annual induction ceremony, set for this Saturday (Nov. 14) event at the Peacock Theatre in Los Angeles.

Liam wrote, “It’s too far to be going for the night I got s–t to do it’s Christmas,” he wrote in response to the report on X Tuesday morning (Nov. 10).

#740. ‘Bugonia,’ ‘Lord of the Flies’ Among 2026 FilmLight Colour Awards Winners

The awards, announced at ToruńCamerimage in Poland, recognize color grading across five categories. Winners will receive a special full-color version of the festival’s Golden Frog trophy.

Yorgos Lanthimos’ Bugonia, Marc Munden’s Lord of the Flies and Hasan Hadi’s The President’s Cake were among the winners of the 2026 FilmLight Colour Awards, announced Saturday at the ToruńCamerimage film festival in Poland.

Bugonia, graded by Greg Fisher of Company 3, took the Theatrical Feature award. Lanthimos’ darkly comic science-fiction thriller stars Emma Stone as a powerful pharmaceutical executive kidnapped by two conspiracy theorists convinced she is an alien plotting to destroy Earth.

Aidan Farrell of The Farm Post Production won the TV Series/Episodic category for Lord of the Flies, Munden’s television adaptation of William Golding’s novel about a group of schoolboys stranded on an uninhabited island whose attempts to establish order descend into savagery. Related Stories Business ITV Unveils "Temporary" Content Cost Cuts as Q3 Ad Revenue Drops 8 Percent Amid "Weaker" Demand Movies 'Long Long Night' Director Youm Kyu-bock on Creating Animation That Takes Kids Seriously

The Spotlight and Documentary award went to The President’s Cake, graded by Andu Radu of Abator. Hadi’s feature, set in 1990s Iraq under Saddam Hussein, follows a young girl tasked with making a cake to celebrate the dictator’s birthday, an assignment that exposes the hardships of life under his regime.

The sixth annual awards recognize excellence in colour grading across five categories: Theatrical Feature, TV Series/Episodic, Spotlight and Documentary, Commercial and Emerging Talent. The winners received a special full-color version of Camerimage’s Golden Frog trophy, created in recognition of the contribution colorists make to the art of cinematography.

In the Commercial category, Nadia Khairat Gómez took the prize for the North Face campaign Defy Easy, while Imri Agmon won Emerging Talent for the Kidsuper SS26 fashion film The Boy Who Jumped the Moon.

The awards were presented as part of TorunCamerimage, the world’s leading festival dedicated to the art of cinematography. Festival founder and director Marek Żydowicz said the awards recognize the creative collaboration between colorists, cinematographers and directors in shaping a film’s visual language.

“Colorists help them achieve this, working together with cinematographers and directors to create emotional depth in film images, balance their colors and enhance color and tonal accents in individual shots,” Żydowicz said.

Commercial: North Face, Defy Easy — Nadia Khairat Gómez

#739. Hideki Shirakawa obituary: chemist who showed that plastics can conduct electricity

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Kazuo Akagi is a research professor at Ritsumeikan University, Kusatsu, Japan, and professor emeritus at Kyoto University and the University of Tsukuba. He worked with Shirakawa on polyacetylene thin films starting in 1984, when he joined Shirakawa’s lab at the University of Tsukuba.

Hideki Shirakawa pioneered the field of conductive polymers, overturning the common view that plastics do not conduct electricity. His demonstration that thin films of polyacetylene — an organic polymer — can become conductive when doped with small amounts of other chemicals earned him a share of the 2000 Nobel Prize in Chemistry (with Alan MacDiarmid and Alan Heeger). He was the second Japanese chemist to receive this award, after Kenichi Fukui in 1981. Shirakawa has died aged 90.

Shirakawa was born in Tokyo. After graduating from secondary school in Takayama City, he studied chemical engineering at the Tokyo Institute of Technology (now the Institute of Science Tokyo). He went on to pursue master’s and doctoral studies there, under the supervision of polymer chemist Shu Kambara, earning a Doctor of Engineering degree for his research on how blocks of organic molecules combine to form polymer chains.

Chemistry education must change to help the planet: here’s how

Chemistry education must change to help the planet: here’s how

After completing his doctorate in 1966, Shirakawa was hired as a research associate in the laboratory of Sakuji Ikeda at Tokyo Tech. There, he began studying how acetylene molecules join together to form a polymer, using Ziegler–Natta catalysts (which are based on organic molecules containing transition metals).

In 1967, Shirakawa was joined in his experiments by a visiting researcher from South Korea, Hyung Chick Pyun. The pair were polymerizing acetylene using a catalyst composed of tetrabutoxytitanium and triethylaluminium to produce powdered polyacetylene.

On one occasion, however, the protocol failed to produce the powder. Instead, a ragged film formed on the surface of the solution in the flask. On closer inspection, it became clear that the visiting researcher had mistakenly used a much higher concentration of the catalyst than was intended — 1,000 times higher. Shirakawa went on to synthesize a thin film of polyacetylene with a metallic lustre by introducing acetylene gas into a flask coated on the inside with the concentrated catalyst.

Chemists struggle to ditch hazardous solvents — even after decades of ‘green’ efforts

Chemists struggle to ditch hazardous solvents — even after decades of ‘green’ efforts

Subsequently, he travelled to the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia, where he worked with MacDiarmid and Heeger. The team discovered that adding small amounts of molecules that accept electrons (such as bromine) or that donate electrons (such as arsenic pentafluoride) increased the electrical conductivity of the thin film by a factor of ten million. This work led to the trio’s Nobel award.

#738. Scientists just found dinosaur blood that survived 115 million years

Scientists have discovered remarkably preserved traces of dinosaur blood inside 115-million-year-old bones, revealing that delicate biological molecules can survive far longer than previously believed. The breakthrough could transform how researchers study prehistoric animals and even influence the search for ancient life beyond Earth.

An international team led by Curtin University found fossilized red blood cells and chemical evidence of blood molecules in the remains of Aratasaurus museunacionali, a meat-eating theropod dinosaur discovered in northeastern Brazil. The findings, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, also include amino acids associated with collagen, an important structural protein found in bones and other connective tissues.

The discovery provides the first definitive chemical confirmation of molecules derived from hemoglobin inside fossilized dinosaur red blood cells. Earlier research had identified structures resembling blood cells in ancient fossils, but scientists had not conclusively demonstrated the presence of these particular molecular remains within them.

Ancient Dinosaur Blood Preserved Inside Fossilized Bones

When researchers examined the dinosaur's limb bones, they identified numerous mineralized red blood cells inside vascular canals, the tiny passages that once contained blood vessels. Chemical analysis revealed preserved heme molecules, which are components of hemoglobin, the protein that allows red blood cells to transport oxygen.

Finding these molecules provided direct chemical evidence that the fossil contained remnants of ancient blood. It also demonstrated that some biological materials once thought too fragile to survive for millions of years can remain detectable under exceptional conditions.

The study was led by John Curtin Distinguished Professor Kliti Grice, founding director of Curtin University's WA-Organic and Isotope Geochemistry Centre and an Australian Research Council Laureate Fellow.

"To detect intact heme-derived molecules in 115-million-year-old red blood cells is astonishing: this really is a landmark discovery," Professor Grice said.

"It not only extends the known fossil record of blood, but also offers a direct molecular window into the physiology of long-extinct animals so we may better understand them and the world they lived in."

How Dinosaur Blood Survived 115 Million Years

The extraordinary preservation appears to be connected to a mineral called hausmannite. This mineral helped stabilize the fossilized blood cells and preserve their molecular components (including amino acids of collagen) over an immense span of geological time.

In effect, the mineral created a natural time capsule that protected microscopic evidence of the dinosaur's biology long after its death.

Researchers believe the conditions surrounding the dinosaur's burial were also crucial. They suspect the animal was quickly covered by sediment in an environment with little oxygen and abundant microbial activity. These conditions may have helped preserve biological material that would ordinarily have broken down and disappeared.

The international research effort brought together scientists from Curtin University's School of Earth and Planetary Sciences, the Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology, the Brazilian National Museum, the Regional University of Cariri, and Johns Hopkins University.

A Discovery That Challenges Fossil Preservation Limits

The findings challenge a longstanding assumption in paleontology that molecules associated with blood, particularly those derived from hemoglobin, could not remain preserved across such enormous periods of time.

Beyond confirming the survival of ancient blood components, the discovery raises the possibility that other fossils may contain molecular information that conventional examinations have overlooked.

"These findings challenge longstanding assumptions that certain biomolecules such as hemoglobin cannot survive deep time," Professor Grice said.

"It opens exciting new avenues for molecular-level paleontology, allowing us to investigate the evolution of blood, metabolism and even activity levels in ancient animals."

Such information could eventually help researchers better understand how extinct animals functioned, including aspects of their metabolism and physiology that are difficult to reconstruct from bones alone.

Implications for Ancient Life Beyond Earth

The significance of the discovery may extend well beyond dinosaurs. Understanding how fragile biological structures can survive for millions of years could also help scientists identify possible traces of ancient life in other extreme environments, including those beyond Earth.

Professor Martin Van Kranendonk, head of Curtin University's School of Earth and Planetary Sciences, said the results are changing how researchers understand the preservation of molecular structures over vast timescales and under harsh conditions.

These insights could be valuable to astrobiology, a field that investigates the possibility of life elsewhere in the universe. If biological molecules or their chemical signatures can persist under the right conditions for more than 100 million years, scientists may need to reconsider where and how they look for evidence of ancient organisms.

"This study exemplifies how coordinated efforts across institutions, continents and scientific disciplines can unlock extraordinary insights into ancient life," Professor Van Kranendonk said.

The research was supported by a 2021 Australian Research Council Laureate Fellowship awarded to Professor Grice.

The study, titled "Heme signatures in mineralized red blood cells within vascular canals of a 115- million-year-old dinosaur bone," was published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

#737. Severe Weather, Radius Clauses and Finding the Next Generation of Festival Headliners: ‘It’s a Year-by-Year Fight to Stay Alive’

Huston Powell, Heather Kolker, Jeremy Shpizner, Melissa Ormond and Allen Scott in conversation at the Billboard Live Music Summit.

Within the last year, the festival space has experienced a more volatile market. Rising production costs and more frequent severe weather events have put events at risk, and at Billboard’s Live Music Summit at the 1 Hotel in West Hollywood, C3 Presents’ Huston Powell remarked, “It’s a year-by-year fight to stay alive.” Explore Billboard See latest videos, charts and news

Joined by Powell, Heather Kolker of Dreamshop Management, Jeremy Shpizner of booking agency ROAM, Melissa Ormond of Goldenvoice and Allen Scott of Another Planet Entertainment and moderated by Billboard senior correspondent Katie Bain, the conversation spanned how to determine a good festival headliner, navigating severe weather, rising costs and the best time to announce a lineup. Related Agents Look Ahead as AI Keeps Advancing: 'We Have the Privilege of Being in a Human Industry' Weezer Honored as Billboard Legends of Live as Rivers Cuomo Reflects on the Road Life: 'A Mission I Want to Take On' Michael Sanft, Attorney Who Represented Keffe D in 2Pac Murder Trial, Dies at 54

For those looking to create their own festival, expenses have only gotten higher in recent years. “The inflation in the United States since 2021 has probably been around 27%,” Scott says. “For Outside Lands specifically, we’ve gone up 60% in our cost. It is extraordinary. And ticket prices can’t keep up with that. You have different price points and additional sponsorship, getting more top-end experiences to keep your general admission ticket price lower.”

Kolker added, “You can get into a situation where you get a festival offer that might make sense for where you are already, but with the cost of buses and crew coming out of COVID, it’s unaffordable.”

To help with keeping ticket prices at a reasonable rate for the average fan while still helping festival promoters make money, Ormond notes premium experiences are becoming more of a necessity. “There’s a segment of the population willing to pay for a higher-end experience, and that helps take some of the pressure off.”

Weather events have also led to festival cancellations. Bonnaroo announced it will be taking a year off in 2027 in order to let the grounds rest for a year following severe weather events in both 2025 and 2026.

“We have been dealing with weather conditions in New Orleans or Western Michigan forever,” Ormond said. “But California — we had never evacuated a festival until Cruel World in 2023. We had never evacuated the desert in 25 years of Coachella, and we evacuated twice in the last six months.”

The science behind determining the best festival headliner has also become more complicated in recent years. As more acts grow into stadiums, those booking festivals note that they’re more so looking for an artist who is going to break.

“You have to adapt,” Powell says. “There’s a certain level of act that disappears off your radar if you’re anybody except Coachella — the Harry Styles, the Justin Biebers — because we don’t spend enough to get those acts. They’re in the stadiums. So you have to try to get ahead of the curve. If you’re lucky, you get those acts who are on that next cycle… They used to say you have to elevate the new headliners. Now we have no choice.”

The first trailer for Other World: A Stranger Things Adventure doesn't show much, but there are enough clues for fans to figure out what it's about here.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

So, you thought "Stranger Things" was done and dusted after all that Conformity Gate nonsense? No way! Netflix's sci-fi sensation returns in the live-action prequel series "Other Worlds: A Stranger Things Adventure."

Created by the Duffer Brothers and Kate Trefry, with the episodes set to be directed by Joe Wright ("Darkest Hour", "Black Mirror"), this new show isn't set in Hawkins or the electric '80s. No, this time around, the action takes place in Marion, Nevada, in 1955, and you know what else is located in Nevada, right? Area 51.

The teaser trailer certainly teases the possibility of a trip to the world's most paradoxically famous secret military base, showcasing a bike and radio resting outside of a fence with a sign that clearly says it's a restricted area (in any TV show or film, that's actually an invitation to see what's on the other side). Of course, the tease doesn't end there, as the thunder booms in the sky and there's a visual hint of a wormhole.

No story details about "Other Worlds: A Stranger Things Adventure" have been released to date, but there are some clues out there for all the Internet sleuths.

Trefrey wrote the Henry Creel-focused "Stranger Things: The First Shadow" play, while Matt Duffer explained to Variety how a spin-off show would tackle the rock that Henry found in the briefcase in "Stranger Things." So, yes, expect this to be a Henry-centric affair and the start of his long, hard road to hell and becoming Vecna.

What'll be interesting, though, is to see how the show ties into the history of Area 51. After all, it was on April 12, 1955, that CIA officer Richard Bissell discovered the site, while the "Other Worlds" trailer has the date of April 19th clearly marked onscreen, so the timelines align nicely here.

"Stranger Things" has never been shy of tying itself to real-world science and historical events, so it'll be fascinating to see how the show explores Area 51 as a concept and the secrets everybody believes are hidden there.

Was it really a site to test highly advanced weapons and aircraft, or was E.T.'s cousin held hostage there until he revealed Colonel Sanders' 11 herbs and spices? Who knows, with all this renewed excitement around this mysterious military facility, we might get another "Storm Area 51" event to enjoy and laugh at all over again.

Regardless, more "Stranger Things" is welcome news, and since it's presumably about one of the show's best characters, Henry Creel, it only adds another layer to his already intriguing lore. If we can't have an origin story about Hopper's incredible and envious moustache, this is the next best thing.

"Other Worlds: A Stranger Things Adventure" arrives on Netflix in 2028.

#734. NASA’s Swift telescope falls to Earth after nearly 22 years in space

NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory has returned to Earth after spending nearly 22 years in space, bringing an extraordinary era of astronomical discovery to a close. The spacecraft re-entered Earth's atmosphere on Wednesday, ending a mission that lasted more than ten times longer than originally planned.

Launched in 2004, Swift was a pioneering space observatory equipped with three telescopes designed to study some of the most powerful explosions in the universe. Its instruments could detect different types of light, allowing scientists to investigate energetic cosmic events that would be difficult to understand using a single telescope.

NASA's Swift Observatory Re-Enters Earth's Atmosphere

The U.S. Space Force confirmed that Swift entered the atmosphere at 7:39 a.m. EST on Wednesday above North Sumatra, Indonesia. The reported location was approximately 3.4 degrees north latitude and 98.6 degrees east longitude.

NASA anticipated that most of the spacecraft would burn up as it plunged through the atmosphere. However, officials acknowledged that some components might have survived the intense heat of re-entry.

A Two-Year NASA Mission That Lasted Nearly 22 Years

Swift was originally developed to investigate gamma-ray bursts, extraordinarily powerful flashes of high-energy radiation associated with some of the most extreme events in the cosmos. These bursts can occur when massive stars collapse or when certain compact objects, such as neutron stars, merge.

Although NASA initially planned for Swift to operate for just two years, the observatory continued making scientific contributions for more than two decades.

One of its most important capabilities was its ability to respond quickly to sudden cosmic events. When Swift detected an energetic outburst, it could rapidly redirect its telescopes toward the source and notify observatories around the world. This coordinated approach allowed astronomers to study brief astronomical phenomena before they faded from view.

Swift also observed multiple wavelengths of light, giving researchers different ways to examine the same event and better understand the physical processes behind it.

Over its remarkably long lifetime, Swift's scientific contributions expanded far beyond its original focus on gamma-ray bursts.

The observatory helped astronomers investigate active galaxies powered by supermassive black holes, stars that produce powerful X-ray flares, and supernovae, the enormous explosions that mark the deaths of certain stars.

Its observations also extended much closer to home, including studies of comets and asteroids within our own solar system.

By combining rapid observations with the ability to detect different forms of radiation, Swift became a valuable tool for exploring both distant cosmic explosions and nearby objects. Its re-entry marks the end of a mission that greatly exceeded its planned lifespan and helped transform scientists' understanding of some of the universe's most energetic phenomena.

Materials provided by NASA. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#733. Hilary Duff Reflects On Her Massive Lucky Me Tour: ‘I’m Really Proud of Myself, and That’s Hard to Feel As An Adult’

The current Billboard cover star received the Outstanding Pop Tour of the Year Award at the 2026 Billboard Live Music Summit in Los Angeles.

Current Billboard cover star Hilary Duff made an appearance at the Billboard Live Music Summit on Tuesday (Nov. 10) at the 1 Hotel West Hollywood to accept the award for Outstanding Pop Tour of the Year and talk about taking this run, The Lucky Me Tour, on the road.

Speaking with Billboard‘s executive editor Lyndsey Havens, Duff reflected on the moments when she decided that she wanted to tour behind her hit album luck… or something, a run that brought her back out on the road after an almost 20-year hiatus from touring.

“I remember sitting with my husband and talking about it, and he’s always the person to calm me down and make everything really digestible,” Duff said. “But then past that I was sitting with my manager Darren [Gilmore] and Colin Lewis at Live Nation and being like, ‘no, I’m gonna do this,’ and just being really scrappy and confident, and then sitting in my car and being like, ‘oh my god, am I gonna do this?’ It was just one foot in front of the other, and then this other part of me that was like, ‘I know how to do this, and I know that I can.’”

Duff has more than proved that she could, with The Lucky Me Tour having grossed $48.3 million from 610,000 tickets sold through its first 40 shows, according to Billboard Boxscore. At the Summit, Duff spoke about how the show has evolved throughout the run, which will continue next year with 32 more dates in arenas across Europe, Latin America and the United States from May through November.

“We’re constantly evolving and changing things,” Duff said. “Like, ‘oh, that really worked this night, let’s lean more into that’, or ‘that song doesn’t fit well there, let’s change that.’ Constantly gut-checking what feels good and lands well with me is what makes it land with other people.”

Duff also spoke about the realities of being away from her four children while on the road, saying that “It’s been a real practice in like, I matter too, and my dreams matter too. It goes against everything in your body to step away from the children that you created. But it’s okay to make sacrifices for your family and still live a life that you find purpose in just for yourself. This has just been a big year of dreaming, and some of those dreams becoming realities.”

She also talked about speaking to her younger selves, from the era when she was a child star on a hit TV show to an internationally famous teenage pop star to an early twenty-something who stepped away from it all to figure her life out.

“It would just be really nice to go back and tell her that she figured it all out in a really healthy way, and that it’s on her terms,” Duff said. “There was a point where when you’re on a train that’s going so fast, it’s hard to stop it, and I didn’t even know why I wanted to stop it — I was just overwhelmed and done. It’s really hard to stop that at that age, and to have enough guts to just need to pause.

“I did eventually pause for a really long time,” she continued, “and I think I would be really proud and be like, ‘Girl, you take a break and figure this out, and you go get an awesome family — [it will be a] roller coaster up and down sometimes, personally and professionally — but all that gets you to a really cool place.’ This has just been such an epic year, a year filled with love, and I’m so proud. I’m really proud of myself, and that’s hard to feel as an adult.”

CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. — NASA has officially launched the Moon Base Student Challenge, asking students to help build humanity's future on the moon. And there's $1 million in prizes up for grabs for the winners.

To build and sustain a base on the moon, NASA will have to solve a myriad of problems. And they're looking to the next generation for help, the space agency's chief Jared Isaacman said Sunday (Nov. 8).

"We are inviting students from across the country to help solve some of the problems that stand between humanity and a permanent presence on another world," Isaacman said. "We're putting 1 million in prizes together to support the best ideas and recognize the teams behind them."

Isaacman made this announcement wearing his blue flight suit from the rocket garden at NASA's Kennedy Space Center Visitor Center amidst the agency's MAX POWER air show event. Just the day before, he flew fighter jets in that suit and even jumped out of a plane, skydiving into the event. Soon after this announcement, he was flying another fighter plane above the crowd.

The audience for this announcement was filled with students of all ages. Some young children wearing costume spacesuits squeezed as close as they could to the front of the room while teenagers considering their futures listened intently. It was clear that Isaacman's presence and words were landing with this group.

But what moon base challenges does NASA want to see these students tackle? In short, all of them.

"The moon base will allow us to conduct groundbreaking science, test new technologies, and prepare again for where we inevitably go next, which is the red planet," he said. "But before any of that can happen, we have an awful lot of problems that need to be solved."

"We need ways to generate power through the long lunar night. We need to protect our astronauts from that incredibly harsh and dangerous and demanding environment on the surface. We need to move people and equipment around on the surface and support human life three days away from Earth," Isaacman said, illustrating just a few of the big issues that present with the concept of a moon base.

This challenge is open to high school and post-secondary students based in the U.S. For participating students, they will form teams that will work on an idea from one of six different technical topics related to creating and running a moon base. These six topics include power systems, habitats, communications, mobility, life support and astronaut safety.

This will be what Isaacman described as a "multi-phase competition that mirrors how ideas are developed actually in the aerospace industry."

"Teams will first submit concepts, then they're going to refine them, and finalists will have the opportunity to present their solutions directly to NASA leaders and stakeholders," he further explained.

"The prize money is great for sure, but the the real opportunity is to work on problems NASA is actively trying to solve right now, so students don't need to wait to graduation to contribute to that effort," Isaacman added.

Right now, NASA has a long road ahead of them before a moon base is actually built. In mid-2027, the agency is planning to launch its Artemis III mission which will see a crew of four astronauts practice rendezvous maneuvers with two different lunar landers. If all goes to plan, this will be followed by Artemis IV landing humans on the moon's surface for the first time since the final Apollo mission in 1972.

The agency is making these big steps forward to not just a crewed return to the moon, but a sustained, long-term return to the moon. However, knowing that a fully-fledged moon base is still firmly in the future, they are banking on the ingenuity, creativity and passion of

If you're a student or know a student interested in participating in this challenge, you can find more information on NASA's website here. Interested students can register until Jan. 25, 2027.

#731. Don't miss: Meteor showers, fireballs, and a supermoon light up November's night sky

November 2026 is packed with celestial events worth watching, from brilliant meteors streaking across the sky to a striking encounter between Mars and Jupiter. NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft is also approaching an extraordinary milestone, while a dazzling supermoon will close out the month.

Three meteor showers offer multiple opportunities to catch shooting stars, including occasional fireballs bright enough to stand out dramatically against the night sky. Meanwhile, two of the solar system's most recognizable planets will appear unusually close together just before sunrise.

As if that weren't enough, humanity's most distant spacecraft is reaching a point where radio signals from Earth take an entire day to arrive.

Here's what NASA recommends watching for in November.

Three Meteor Showers Could Light Up November's Sky

November gives skywatchers several chances to see meteors flash across the darkness. The first opportunities come from the Southern and Northern Taurids, two related meteor showers that reach their highest activity levels about a week apart.

The Southern Taurids peak around November 5, followed by the Northern Taurids around November 12. Both showers get their names from the constellation Taurus, where their meteors appear to originate when viewed from Earth.

Neither shower is especially prolific. Even under excellent conditions, each typically produces only about five meteors per hour. However, the Taurids are known for occasionally producing impressive fireballs, exceptionally bright meteors that can make even a relatively quiet night of skywatching memorable.

The Leonids provide another opportunity later in the month. Their best viewing periods are expected during the early morning hours of November 17 and 18, particularly after the Moon has disappeared below the horizon. Under ideal conditions, observers could see approximately 15 meteors per hour, although actual counts will generally be lower.

For the best chance of spotting meteors, travel somewhere away from bright city lights. Allow your eyes roughly 30 minutes to become accustomed to the darkness, then watch a broad section of the sky rather than concentrating on one small area.

Mars and Jupiter Appear Almost Side by Side

Meteor showers aren't the only reason to get outside before dawn. On November 15 and 16, Mars and Jupiter will create an eye-catching pairing in the southeastern sky.

The two planets will appear separated by only about 1.2 degrees, slightly more than the apparent width of two full Moons placed next to each other.

Jupiter will be the brighter of the two, making it relatively easy to identify. Nearby, Mars will stand out with its characteristic reddish appearance.

No telescope or binoculars will be necessary to enjoy the sight. Both planets should be readily visible to the unaided eye under suitable viewing conditions.

Although they will appear remarkably close from Earth's perspective, Mars and Jupiter remain separated by enormous distances in space. Their apparent proximity is simply a result of their positions along our line of sight.

Watching the planets over several consecutive mornings will reveal another interesting feature of their motion. They will gradually appear to move closer together before their positions shift and they begin separating again.

Voyager 1 Reaches an Extraordinary Deep Space Milestone

While November offers plenty to observe in Earth's skies, something equally remarkable is happening far beyond the planets.

NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft is reaching a historic distance of one light-day from Earth, becoming the first human-made object ever to travel that far from our planet.

A light-day is the distance light travels through space in 24 hours. Because radio signals move at the speed of light, a message transmitted from Earth will require an entire day to reach Voyager 1 at that distance.

If the spacecraft sends a response immediately, the return signal will take another 24 hours to arrive. That means even the fastest possible round-trip communication will require approximately 48 hours.

The milestone illustrates just how far Voyager 1 has traveled since leaving Earth and how challenging it has become to communicate with a spacecraft exploring such distant regions of space.

To get a sense of the spacecraft's current direction, look toward the constellation Ophiuchus, also known as the Serpent Bearer. Voyager 1 is traveling through space in that general direction, far beyond anything visible to the unaided eye.

NASA is marking the achievement on November 17 with its Shine Bright for Voyager's Light-Day activation, inviting people to celebrate this extraordinary accomplishment in space exploration.

November's Supermoon Begins a Three-Month Celestial Show

The final major skywatching highlight arrives on November 24, when a full supermoon will rise into the evening sky.

A supermoon occurs when a full Moon coincides with a period when the Moon is relatively close to Earth in its orbit. Because the Moon follows a slightly elliptical path rather than a perfect circle, its distance from our planet changes throughout the month.

When a full Moon occurs near the closer portion of that orbit, it can appear somewhat larger and brighter than an average full Moon. Although the difference is real, it is often subtle enough that casual observers may not immediately notice it.

November's event is particularly noteworthy because it begins a sequence of three consecutive supermoons. Another will follow in December, with a third arriving in January.

For an especially memorable view, NASA recommends looking toward the eastern horizon around sunset on November 24, when the full Moon will be rising.

The Moon may seem unusually enormous when it first appears near the horizon. However, much of that dramatic impression comes from a familiar visual phenomenon called the Moon illusion.

This optical effect makes the Moon appear larger when it is close to the horizon than when it is high overhead, even though its actual apparent size changes very little. The illusion can occur during any full Moon, not just a supermoon.

With three meteor showers, a close planetary pairing, a historic Voyager 1 milestone, and the beginning of a supermoon series, November offers plenty of reasons to look up and explore the night sky.

Materials provided by NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
