#730. ‘Apart’ Star Luca Pasqualino and Creator Stelana Kliris Unpack a Love Story Amid War and Apartheid

The film, starring Leem Lubany and inspired by the experiences of the writer-director's parents who emigrated from Cyprus to South Africa, opens Tallinn's Critics' Picks program.

South African Cypriot writer-director Stelana Kliris’ parents emigrated from Cyprus and moved to South Africa, leaving one divided country for another. What is that experience like, you wonder? Now, you can go on a cinematic journey to travel back in time and across the world to find out. Kliris (Find Me Falling, Committed) has used the experiences of her refugee parents as inspiration and “translated this into a film that challenges the idea of ‘us’ and ‘them.'”

Apart is the movie‘s fitting title, and it stars Leem Lubany (Omar, Rock the Kasbah), Luca Pasqualino (Rivals, The Musketeers) and Girley Jazama (Under the Hanging Tree, The White Line). And with war and refugees constantly in the headlines, the film explores issues and challenges that feel particularly timely and topical. Related Stories Movies 'Bugonia,' 'Lord of the Flies' Among 2026 FilmLight Colour Awards Winners Business ITV Unveils "Temporary" Content Cost Cuts as Q3 Ad Revenue Drops 8 Percent Amid "Weaker" Demand

Apart will get its world premiere at the 30th edition of the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival (PÖFF) in Estonia on Friday, Nov. 13, opening its Critics’ Picks section.

“In 1974, when Turkey invades Cyprus, young Eleni (Lubany) leaves her homeland through an arranged marriage and finds herself in Apartheid South Africa, swapping one divided country for another,” teases a synopsis for the film. “There, a new life with Nico (Pasqualino) slowly turns into love, until an unexpected friendship forces her to confront a secret from her past.”

Kliris wrote and directed Apart and produced it with Susan Simnett, Jamie Harvey and Ioanna Bolomyti. The cinematographer is Simon Sarketzis, with Emilios Avraam handling editing. Reinvent Yellow Sales is handling sales. Watch a trailer for Apart right here.

Pasqualino, who is now back on Disney+ in the second part of season 2 of the hit show Rivals, and Kliris talked to THR about Apart, how it was shot in Cyprus and captures a 1970s aesthetic, casting challenges, and how urgent the themes explored in the film feel.

Stelana, how much of Apart is based on your family’s history and experience?

STELANA KLIRIS My parents are both from Cyprus. My mom was a refugee from the war, and they actually met in South Africa. I was born and raised there. I experienced Apartheid as a child as I grew up during the ’80s in South Africa. So I grew up with all of these stories from both my parents and my own experiences. The film was an opportunity to bring all of that together.

How did Luca come aboard, especially given his busy TV schedule?

STELANA KLIRIS Luca was just an absolute gem to find. We worked with casting director Nancy Bishop, but it’s a difficult film, politically and historically, and a lot of local talent was a little fearful of taking on the subject matter. So we went outside the island [of Cyprus], and I’m so glad we did.

Luca, how did you get into your character, Nico, and his struggles?

LUCA PASQUALINO I don’t come from a Cypriot or South African background, but I do come from an immigrant Italian background. So I’ve been very much brought up around these stories. My grandparents immigrated to England from Italy after the war and then had to go through the struggles of not being from that nation. They sacrificed so much and had to forget everything that they’d ever known, leave it all behind to create a better life for themselves. That part of Nico is part of my family’s history.

And it wasn’t just the financial struggles they faced, but also not knowing the language, not knowing anything about the country. They literally had to start again. So that part of the story very much resonated with me.

Apart has characters who are not black-and-white but complicated. For example, with Nico, I loved some of the things he says or does and hated others…

STELANA KLIRIS Yes, they are very complex characters. They are very flawed and human. That was very important to me. They are not based on a specific person, but [inspired by] all these characters and people that I grew up with who were never perfect and sometimes had to do something that is maybe a little wrong to survive.

It’s a very human element, and what’s great about both Luca and Leem is that they really brought out this complexity. These characters are very three-dimensional, and they were able to really bring them to life in this way. With Luca, you get to see this really great range, because he can be very vulnerable, but his character can also be really hard, and [over time] we understand why.

LUCA PASQUALINO Nico is a very proud man. It would break his heart if he wasn’t giving his family the best that he could possibly give them. So, yes, there’s a moral ambiguity to it. The rules are there to maybe be bent or broken in certain ways, and he denies it a lot of the time. But there comes a moment where something shifts in him and he realizes he needs to take risks in life. And he decides that he’s going to go down a slightly alternative route. He does what he feels that he has to do. He has a wife, and he has to provide and care and take matters into his own hands.

Did you have an accent coach or so, Luca? How did you develop the way Nico sounds?

LUCA PASQUALINO We got there with a lot of time, a lot of repetition and a lot of frustration at times. It takes a lot of hard work when you don’t speak the language. It’s difficult to understand intonation and the flow of dialogue. Early on, our dialect coach would say a line to me, and I thought I said it exactly how she did. But she said no. To my ear, it sounded exactly the same, but to hers it didn’t. So, I hope it’s not awful. I’m happy I got to have that experience, and I hope people can understand everything that we’re trying to say.

STELANA KLIRIS They worked with a really great dialect coach called Léa Maléni, and Luca had to learn Greek. And they had to speak with an accent. We had multiple dialect coaches. Girley Jazama is actually Namibian, so she had to learn to speak Sesotho. We had Turkish Cypriot actors on set, some of whom didn’t speak any English. So at some point, we had about three or four different dialect coaches and interpreters on set. And in between takes, trying to give notes and talking about the scene just became this cacophony of languages. It was a great multinational experience.

Was there any scene that was particularly difficult to shoot?

LUCA PASQUALINO Every day was a new challenge. I loved it. But the one thing that stands out the most was just trying to make one scene feel as tragic as possible. There’s a moment where Nico talks about his brother and how he was kidnapped and murdered. At one point, I fell into this hole of overthinking it. But a couple of days before [we shot it], I decided I knew the lines, but I was not going to think about it anymore. And then the day we shot that scene, I was just open to allowing it to happen. There is a moment that was not scripted. I just had to feel that heartbreak within me instead of trying to act.

Stelana, can you tell me a bit about the visual aesthetic of the film and where you shot it? There are scenes that look a bit like an old home video…

STELANA KLIRIS We shot all of it in Cyprus. We were supposed to shoot in South Africa as well, but it didn’t work out in the end, for various reasons. Cyprus still has a lot of ’70s aesthetics in terms of buildings and neighborhoods, but we did have to hide a lot of things. And whatever we didn’t manage to hide had to be erased with VFX.

We also used an 8-millimeter camera for a lot of scenes to give it that lovely ’70s home video look. In fact, a party scene in an apartment is an exact replica of home videos I have from my parents, where immigrant Cypriots gathered in little apartments and squeezed together, having parties. We used some archive footage as well, just to really make it as authentic as possible and really show South Africa in the ’70s. We’ve mixed it up. Some of it is our own, some of it is archive. Hopefully, you can’t really tell. It’s just all there to immerse people in that era.

Apart is a historic snapshot, but it also feels quite timely. Or maybe it’s timeless? What do you think?

STELANA KLIRIS I think it’s very relevant. I think everyone can relate to being young and struggling and trying to find your way in the world, regardless of the era or whether there’s a backdrop of war. It’s a very human story and very intimate. And it really tries to boil down to a human level the many problems that we still have, the same problems that we’ve had throughout history.

LUCA PASQUALINO All you have to do is turn on the news, and you can see that it’s happening all over the world. The unfortunate, sad reality is that for a lot of people, there is always something to fight over. Even if you were to take the war element out of the script, there are still so many other things going on.

The relationship between Nico and Eleni is the real heart of the film. It’s two people who, for their own reasons, are trying to find a better life, trying to escape, and they end up finding solace in each other. The war is the backdrop for a really emotional, heart-wrenching love story.

#729. Global Touring’s Growth Is Being Slowed By Lack of Infrastructure, Live Music Professionals Warn

At the 2026 Billboard Live Music Summit, live entertainment promoters and venue developers discuss the difficulties of breaking into new markets without more venues.

The number of touring markets continues to expanding across the globe, but live entertainment professionals believe the infrastructure has not yet caught up. With the advent of streaming, artists are able to grow their audiences far beyond their own country’s borders, but not all countries are able to accommodate the demand.

Across the globe, agents and promoters are having to book tours years in advance because the limited number of venues in emerging markets is so slim. Related Severe Weather, Radius Clauses and Finding the Next Generation of Festival Headliners: 'It's a Year-by-Year Fight to Stay Alive' Ariel King

“We really need more infrastructure from every country,” OCESA director of international events Guillermo “Memo” Parra said at the 2026 Billboard Live Music Summit today (Nov. 10). Mexico “was ahead of the curve regarding South America because of the Olympics and some other special events. Mexico had infrastructure. It was old, but they had infrastructure.”

On the International Touring Panel moderated by Billboard co-chief content officer Leila Cobo, AEG’s senior vp of global touring Angie Rho added that the promoter is looking to meet the demand in Asia, but is also facing a lack of event spaces. “You might have desire. You might have willingness. You might have fans, but we need venues,” Rho said.

Steve Collins, president of global venue development at Oak View Group told the audience that for every 10 buildings the company proposes, only one or two will come to fruition. Public funding for concert venues, Collins said, is not a popular model, so OVG looks into local partners in global markets to produce new buildings.

“Any market outside the U.S. is really tough to get these buildings done,” Collins said. “Whoever our partner is, you’re not going to take the risk. We’ll figure it out. We’ve become really good at commercializing these buildings and making them work standalone rather than putting our hand out as the first measure.”

Collins pointed to two music-first venues OVG is currently developing in Dublin and Madrid as examples. Both of these developing venues will not have sports tenants and therefore be purpose built to artists and music fans, as well as have more availability for concert nights.

Live Nation global tour promoter Nidhish Varughese said that the company has been focusing on growth in India, which has seen a series of record-breaking shows in recent years.

“With India specifically, we’re doing more shows there. Traditionally, it was always just a two-market play, whether it’s Delhi or Mumbai. But now there’s multiple markets that artists are trying to perform in,” he said at the panel held in Los Angeles. Varughese explained that Live Nation tested the demand with concerts at racetracks in India and discovered there was a huge appetite for more large-scale concerts. Live Nation is now working alongside OVG to find appropriate locations for arenas in the country.

“There’s a lot of territories like in Central Asia where governments are realizing [concerts] could be a good vehicle for tourism,” added Varughese, pointing to Shakira’s recent stop in Kyrgyzstan where the government helped fund the show. “People travel to that region to watch the show. So, it’s a win-win for the artists, where they get to go to a new market. We unlock the new market, discover new audiences and [are] also serving the audiences that have always been there.”

For Rho, Andrea Bocelli’s 2026 performances in Indonesia not only helped broaden AEG’s involvement in the country, but created a once-in-a-lifetime experience for the Italian singer. “It is a place where one of my colleagues almost stepped on a five-foot snake,” Rho joked. “So, even when you have five-foot snake danger, you are also – the flip side of that coin – producing and putting on these performances that are going to be, in an artist’s mind, he’s going to look back on this as a capstone.”

Even in Mexico, where OCESA has seen continued growth, new markets are emerging as artist’s create more routing. Parra explained that Shakira’s record-breaking Las Mujeres Ya No Lloran World Tour played cities in Mexico that he says, “I’ve never even been to.”

But, Parra added, there are only a handful of acts who could pull off the feats Shakira did in Mexico, because of the lack of structure and because of the importance of soccer in the country. “They [would] rather have football instead of concerts because the field will get damaged, and they don’t want to move their games,” Parra said. “So it’s hard to do shows in some other parts of Mexico.”

#728. ‘NAZA’ Tops 1.5 Million Admissions Worldwide

Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor's award-winning exposé on Israel's war in Gaza has grossed more than $14 million at the box office to date.

NAZA hit a new box office milestone, with more than 1.5 million theatrical admissions worldwide.

The award-winning documentary from Israeli film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor looks at the alleged policies the Israeli Defense Force (IDF) uses to target and kill civilians in Gaza.

As of Friday, Nov. 6, NAZA racked up more than 1.54 million theatrical admissions across 47 territories, making it one of the most-watched theatrical docs of 2026.

The film premiered in Venice where it won the Special Jury Prize for directors Abraham and Szor. It was attacked by the right-wing in Israel. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called for the identification and prosecution of the film’s whistle-blower interviewees, and Israel’s culture minister threatened to strip the NAZA directors of their citizenship. Related Stories Movies 'Apart' Star Luca Pasqualino and Creator Stelana Kliris Unpack the Love Story Amid War and Apartheid Movies 'Bugonia,' 'Lord of the Flies' Among 2026 FilmLight Colour Awards Winners

In box office terms, the producers report a total take of more than $14 million, with $1 million and counting coming from the U.S., and $13.5 million in international gross. Michael Tuckman’s mTuckman Media intially started a self release of NAZA in the U.S. on Sept. 30 before Neon came on in late October to expand the film’s theatrical release.

The strongest performance has been in Italy, where NAZA bowed at number one on Sept. 29 via distributor I Wonder. The film has grossed more than $6 million to date, making it the third most-watched documentary in the territory, behind only Fahrenheit 9/11 and The March of the Penguins.

In France, where the film received a special 48-hours event release, to get around French windowing rules, NAZA sold more than 82,000 tickets, topping the box office over the two days.

The film has topped 100,000 admissions in the UK and Ireland, via distributor Dogwoof, and across Benelux via Cherry Pickers. It’s sold more than 80,000 tickets in Germany, more than 60,000 in Spain, and over 50, 000 in Switzerland. impressive figures for a documentary.

The Guardian, which was a producer on NAZA, will screen the film screen for free on its website from early December.

#727. Comets may have destroyed life's ingredients instead of delivering them to Earth

For nearly a century, scientists have considered the possibility that comets helped make life on Earth possible by delivering essential organic molecules from space. Now, new research suggests this long-standing explanation is extremely unlikely.

Comets are known to contain many of the chemical compounds associated with the origins of life. These substances, often called prebiotic molecules, can participate in the chemical reactions that eventually produce the complex ingredients needed for living organisms. For decades, researchers have proposed that comets striking the early Earth supplied a steady stream of these compounds.

However, a new study led by the University of Cambridge challenges that theory. Using advanced computer simulations, researchers found that comets generally approach Earth at speeds and angles that make it extremely difficult for delicate organic molecules to survive. Instead of delivering their chemical cargo intact, most would likely destroy it during their violent arrival.

The findings, published in Scientific Reports, suggest that successful delivery of life's building blocks by comets would have been an extraordinarily rare event. Interestingly, the researchers also found that Mars may have offered somewhat better conditions for receiving these molecules, although the likelihood remains very low.

"Historically, scientists thought that comets were important for the origin of life on Earth, because they carried carbon and nitrogen-bearing molecules, so these giant space snowballs were almost like a 'get out of jail free card' that brought all the molecules a planet would need to seed life," said lead author Dr. Richard Anslow from Cambridge's Institute of Astronomy. "It's kind of a romantic idea, but our results suggest it's highly unlikely."

Why Comets May Have Failed to Deliver Life's Building Blocks

The idea that comets could transport the ingredients for life received renewed attention in 2023, when Anslow and several colleagues explored how these icy objects might behave in planetary systems where worlds orbit relatively close together.

Their earlier research suggested that comets could potentially lose speed as they passed between neighboring planets. Through a series of gravitational encounters, a comet might effectively bounce from one planet to another, eventually traveling slowly enough to deliver organic molecules without destroying them.

The team wanted to determine whether a similar process could have occurred in our own Solar System, potentially explaining how essential chemicals reached the young Earth.

"We're learning more and more all the time about how our Solar System and the Earth formed, and pulling this together with lots of different advances in modeling, which allowed us to investigate this idea that has been around for close to a century," he said.

To investigate, the researchers combined several sophisticated modeling techniques. These included simulations of comet impacts, calculations of how comets interact with planetary atmospheres, and models tracing how comet populations formed and changed as the Solar System developed.

The results revealed a major obstacle. Although a comet might occasionally approach Earth under conditions favorable for preserving organic compounds, such encounters would have been exceptionally uncommon. Successful delivery could not be completely ruled out, but the simulations indicated that it was highly improbable.

A Critical Ingredient for Life Faces Nearly Impossible Odds

To better understand what happens to the molecules carried by comets, the team concentrated on hydrogen cyanide (HCN), a chemical commonly detected in comets throughout our Solar System.

Despite its reputation as a highly toxic substance, hydrogen cyanide is important in research on the origins of life. It contains carbon and nitrogen and can participate in reactions that produce more complex organic compounds, making it a potentially valuable ingredient in the chemistry that preceded living organisms.

The simulations showed that even when hydrogen cyanide managed to survive a comet's arrival, another major problem remained. The impact would need to deposit enough of the molecule in one location to support meaningful chemical reactions. Events capable of producing those useful concentrations were extraordinarily rare.

Timing created yet another difficulty. Comet impacts were much more common during Earth's earliest history, but their frequency declined sharply over the planet's first 500 million years. According to the researchers, there may have been only a handful of opportunities during that entire early period for comets to deliver hydrogen cyanide under favorable conditions.

Even a successful delivery would not necessarily have helped life develop. Hydrogen cyanide deposited on Earth's surface would likely have dispersed or become diluted relatively quickly, leaving little time for the chemical reactions associated with life's origins to get underway.

For the comet theory to work, several unlikely events would therefore have needed to occur together. A comet would have had to strike at just the right speed and angle, preserve its organic cargo, deposit enough material in a suitable location, and trigger important chemical processes before those molecules dispersed.

"It would really have to be a one-in-a-million occurrence, because not only would you need an impact at just the right speed and just the right angle, you would also need everything to happen after that point, in terms of the concentration and the speed at which the chemical origins of life got going," said Anslow. "We can't rule out for certain that it happened that way. But it seems to be a really rare occurrence - at best, a one-off fluke."

If Not Comets, Where Did Life's Ingredients Come From?

The findings raise a fundamental question about Earth's earliest history. If comets were unlikely to supply the chemical building blocks of life, what was responsible?

One possibility involves asteroids, which collided with the early Earth far more frequently than comets. The researchers suggest that asteroid impacts could have created conditions in which important prebiotic molecules formed through chemical reactions associated with those collisions.

Another explanation is that Earth produced these compounds on its own. Natural chemical processes operating on the young planet may have generated the ingredients necessary for increasingly complex chemistry, without requiring organic molecules to arrive from space.

These possibilities do not establish exactly how life began. Instead, they highlight alternative ways that the raw materials for life could have become available on Earth.

Why Mars May Have Had a Better Chance Than Earth

While the simulations cast serious doubt on cometary delivery to Earth, they also revealed an intriguing possibility involving Mars.

The Red Planet is smaller than Earth and currently has a much thinner atmosphere. These characteristics make it a potentially more favorable destination for cometary molecules, since incoming objects could be more likely to reach its surface without completely destroying their chemical cargo.

According to the researchers, Mars may therefore have been better positioned to receive prebiotic compounds during the Solar System's early development, when comet encounters were considerably more frequent.

However, the simulations do not demonstrate that such deliveries actually occurred. Even on Mars, the conditions required for a successful transfer of life's chemical ingredients appear difficult to achieve.

"This is not to say it definitely happened on Mars, of course, but suggests it would be unlikely if it happened on Earth and didn't happen on Mars," said Anslow. "Or the other, perhaps more likely, alternative, is that it didn't happen on either planet."

What the Discovery Means for the Search for Alien Life

Beyond changing how scientists think about Earth's early chemistry, the findings could help guide the search for potentially habitable planets in other star systems.

Future space observatories may be able to investigate distant worlds in greater detail, searching for atmospheric clues that could indicate environments suitable for life. Among the proposed missions is the Habitable Worlds Observatory, a potential successor to the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST).

The researchers suggest that planetary systems where comets can move between closely spaced planets while gradually losing speed may deserve particular attention. In such environments, the unusual comet delivery mechanism explored in their earlier research could be more likely to operate.

Identifying these systems could help astronomers focus future observations on planets where essential organic molecules may have had a better chance of surviving their journey through space.

Although the new findings make comets an unlikely explanation for how life's building blocks reached Earth, they do not eliminate the possibility that cometary delivery played a role elsewhere. Understanding where these chemical transfers are possible could provide valuable clues as scientists continue investigating how life emerges across the universe.

The research received partial support from the Royal Society, the Leverhulme Centre for Life in the Universe, and the Science and Technology Facilities Council (STFC), which is part of UK Research and Innovation (UKRI).

Starfish Space's first Otter has died, just a month after it reached the final frontier.

The Seattle startup announced on Tuesday (Nov. 3) that its Otter 24C satellite suffered a glitch in low Earth orbit (LEO) and is not recoverable.

The anomaly killed an ambitious mission in the cradle, as Otter 24C was still in the commissioning phase.

Otter 24C launched Oct. 1 on SpaceX's Transporter-18 mission, a rideshare flight that carried a total of 130 payloads to LEO (including a prototype satellite for Project Suncatcher, Google's planned AI constellation).

The Starfish satellite was flying a mission for NASA called Small Spacecraft Propulsion and Inspection Capability, or SSPICY for short. The goal was to "demonstrate technologies necessary for future debris-removal missions as well as for future applications in the servicing and inspection of active spacecraft," according to NASA's SSPICY site.

"This advances NASA's in-space manufacturing and assembly (ISAM) goals to ensure a sustainable space operating environment and builds towards a future where objects can be assembled, repaired and maintained in space, significantly expanding possibilities for science and human exploration," the agency added.

Starfish Space was a natural partner. The Seattle company plans to become a big player in the nascent field of satellite servicing, using its line of Otter craft to repair, refuel or deorbit other satellites for a variety of customers.

SSPICY marked Otter's spaceflight debut. The mission plan called for the 739-pound (335-kilogram) Otter 24C spacecraft to approach and inspect "up to four inoperable space objects of U.S. origin" over the course of a two-year mission, performing detailed visual inspections.

But Otter 24C never got the chance to perform any of these orbital rendezvous.

"While working through commissioning steps, Starfish eventually stopped receiving data from Otter 24C," the company said in a Nov. 3 X post.

"An investigation into the loss of communications has determined that fault protection on the satellite bus provided by [California company] Astro Digital had an error that turned off the radio and prevented re-establishing communications," Starfish added. "Starfish, NASA, and Astro Digital have concluded that Otter 24C is not recoverable."

The company further said that it's implementing fixes to reduce the chances that the problem will crop up in the future. And it stressed that Otter 24C's death will not be in vain.

"The work completed through Otter 24C will directly contribute to the success of future Otter missions, as Starfish continues developing the technologies and operations required to make satellite servicing a routine capability in orbit," Starfish said.

Otter Pup 2 is now operating as close as 25 meters away from @GilmourSpace's ElaraSat, fully autonomously. This vid contains imagery captured when we were separated by just 33.6 meters. We’ve demonstrated our ability to safely and precisely operate at very close range, executing intricate maneuvers, gathering detailed imagery, and testing the capabilities we’ll need for docking. With this progress, Otter Pup 2 has officially completed Characterize, the penultimate phase of its mission. That leaves just one phase left: attempting docking, and a chance to make history.October 27, 2026

The Seattle company has other work to do in LEO at the moment as well: Its Otter Pup 2 prototype craft is currently gearing up to conduct a historic docking of its own in LEO.

Otter Pup 2, which launched in June 2025, has been getting closer and closer to another private spacecraft, Gilmour Space's ElaraSat. Last week, the company announced that Otter Pup 2 got within a mere 82 feet (25 meters) of its target.

"With this progress, Otter Pup 2 has officially completed Characterize, the penultimate phase of its mission. That leaves just one phase left: attempting docking, and a chance to make history," Starfish Space said in an Oct. 27 X post.

Two private satellites have docked before, but only much higher above Earth, in geostationary orbit. Such a meetup has not yet happened in LEO.

#725. Janet Jackson ‘So Excited’ in Surprise ‘DWTS’ Cameo Honoring Former ‘All For You’ Video Dancer: ‘I Feel So Honored’

Ms. Jackson beamed into the show on Tuesday night (Nov. 10) for the competition's Grammy Night episode.

Jenna Dewan had a very special, surprise guest on her side on Tuesday night’s (Nov. 10) Dancing With the Stars. The Step Up star and her professional dance partner paid tribute to the Grammy Night theme by dancing to Janet Jackson‘s Billboard Hot 100 No. 1 “All For You,” which won best dance recording at the 2002 Grammy Awards.

In the intro video, Dewan said she was “so excited” for her performance because she recalled dancing with *NSYNC at the Grammy Awards in 2002 and how much that gig meant to her. “It was amazing and it’s the top awards show that you can ever perform at,” she said. Then she heaped praise on Jackson, noting that working for Janet was “the start of my career,” recalling that she danced in two videos for the singer — ”Doesn’t Really Matter” and “All For You” — as well as being a backup dancer on her tours. “This is a full-circle moment.”

The circle remained unbroken when Jackson made an unannounced cameo on the show after Dewan’s high-energy routine to “All For You,” when the singer showed up in a loving message honoring her former dancer. “I am so excited. I cannot wait to watch you perform tonight,” said Jackson, wearing oversized round glasses, a black hoodie and a black and white “Funkbox NYC” ball cap in a video of the moment posted by E! News.

“You’re performing to ‘All For You.’ I feel so honored. ‘All For You!,” Jackson, 60, added with a smile. “I really do feel honored though. I know you’re going to do an incredible job. Weren’t those such fun times we had back then during those days, the All For You tour? I miss you, I love you, I can’t wait to see you tonight, like I said, you’re going to do an incredible job, I know it.”

After scoring a perfect 40 last week for their quickstep to the Beauty and the Beast classic “Be Our Guest” on Disney Night, Dewan and partner Val Chmerkovskiy hit the stage for a jazz routine to “All For You” featuring acrobatic lifts, spins and the kind crisp, fluid choreo Dewan (and Jackson) are known for.

The pair got a score of 28 out of 30 from the judges with Carrie Ann Inaba saying it felt like “no time has passed at all … I expected greatness and you delivered.” In the end, though, despite landing the second-highest score of the night and winning their dance battle against Tatyana Ali and Jan Ravnik, Dewan and Chmerkovskiy were eliminated at show’s end.

Next week’s semifinal show will feature the remaining couples dancing twice. DWTS airs live on Tuesdays at 8 p.m. ET on ABC and Disney+ and streams the next day on Hulu.

#724. A mysterious 93-billion-mile cosmic structure may be the wreckage of colliding worlds

A mysterious structure stretching roughly 93 billion miles across space is giving astronomers new clues about the violent events that shape young planetary systems. Known as the "Cat's Tail," this enormous cloud of dark material lies about 63 light-years from Earth, in the faint constellation Pictor (which is Latin for "painter"). For the past two years, its unusual appearance and uncertain origins have puzzled scientists.

The structure is part of a vast disk of dust and debris surrounding Beta Pictoris, a young star system that resembles our own solar system during its early development. Now, using NASA's Hubble Space Telescope, astronomers have captured previously hidden details of the Cat's Tail in visible light for the first time.

The discovery is described in a study published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters. Led by University of Arizona planetary scientist Arin Avsar, the research team combined the new Hubble images with observations spanning more than 14 years. Their findings provide a clearer picture of the structure's composition, location, and shape, along with additional evidence that a massive collision may have created it.

A Possible Collision Between Pluto-Sized Worlds

"The Cat's Tail is thought to be the aftermath of a collision between large bodies - think something like Pluto," said Avsar, a doctoral student working with the research groups of Daniel Apai and Kevin Wagner at the University of Arizona's Lunar and Planetary Laboratory and Steward Observatory.

"Oddly, this feature had previously only been seen with the James Webb Space Telescope, which detects infrared light, but remained invisible at shorter wavelengths, which has puzzled the community for a while."

The mystery becomes even more interesting when viewed in the context of how planetary systems form.

Today, our solar system appears relatively orderly. Planets follow established paths around the Sun, while many smaller rocky objects occupy "designated" regions such as the asteroid belt. But 4.6 billion years ago, the situation was dramatically different.

A young sun was surrounded by a swirling disk of gas and dust. Rocky objects repeatedly collided, sometimes breaking apart and sometimes combining into larger bodies. Over time, some accumulated enough material to become planets, while countless others were destroyed or scattered.

Astronomers study younger systems like Beta Pictoris because they offer an opportunity to observe processes that unfolded in our own cosmic neighborhood billions of years ago. Its debris disk, consisting of dust and fragments left behind during planetary development, is believed to be approaching the final stages of planet formation.

Why Hubble Could Finally See the Mysterious Cat's Tail

One of the most intriguing questions about the Cat's Tail is why it was previously detectable in infrared light but so difficult to observe in visible light.

The answer may lie in the unusual material that makes up the enormous structure.

"We think the Cat's Tail has eluded our observations in visible light until now because of what it's made of," Avsar explained. "It consists almost entirely of we call organic refractory material, which is heavily carbon-based. These long chains of carbon atoms absorb visible light, so they're quite black."

Organic refractory material consists of complex carbon compounds that can withstand relatively harsh conditions in space. Because these compounds absorb much of the visible light that strikes them, they can make the surrounding dust appear exceptionally dark.

The Hubble observations also support another unusual finding: the Cat's Tail appears to be composed of extremely small, surprisingly porous dust particles.

Individual grains measure only about a micron across, roughly one millionth of a meter. Yet instead of being compact and solid, they appear remarkably "fluffy," with substantial empty space within their structures.

The scale of the entire cloud is difficult to imagine. It may stretch as far as 1,000 astronomical units, with one astronomical unit (AU) defined as the average distance between Earth and the Sun. That corresponds to approximately 93 billion miles, or the equivalent of lining up around 200 trillion house cats from tail to nose.

"How you can get dust grains that small that are as porous as we see here, no one really understands, and that's part of why we study this feature," Avsar said.

How a Violent Collision Could Create Fluffy Cosmic Dust

If the Cat's Tail really formed when large planetary bodies smashed into each other, researchers still need to explain how that destruction produced such tiny, porous particles.

One possibility is that the collision was powerful enough to vaporize some of the material involved.

"It's possible that the velocities involved in the collisions were so high that the carbon grains vaporized, turned into gas, and then recondensed as they cooled, and that's how they became so porous," said co-author Wagner, a NASA Sagan Postdoctoral Fellow at the University of Arizona's Steward Observatory.

In this scenario, the intense impact would have transformed solid carbon material into gas. As the material cooled, it could have condensed back into solid particles with unusually open, lightweight structures.

However, the precise process remains uncertain, and additional observations will be needed to determine whether this explanation is correct.

A 93-Billion-Mile Structure With an Unexpected Shape

The new research also challenges previous assumptions about where the Cat's Tail extends in space.

By combining visible light observations from Hubble with infrared measurements from the James Webb Space Telescope, the researchers used computer modeling to reconstruct the structure's possible three-dimensional arrangement.

Earlier observations suggested that the Cat's Tail extended outward from Beta Pictoris and far behind the star from Earth's perspective. Because the surrounding debris disk is viewed nearly edge-on, it was difficult to determine how much of the structure extended away from us rather than across our field of view.

The new analysis points to a different explanation.

"We find that instead of extending for 1,000 astronomical units behind the star, the Cat's Tail may extend straight sideways relative to us, and there is no third dimension to it," Avsar said. "It's essentially in the same plane of the sky as the star and possibly extends a little bit behind it."

This suggests the structure may be spread mainly across the sky as seen from Earth, rather than projecting deep into space behind the star.

The revised geometry gives astronomers a better understanding of where the dust is located and could help them reconstruct the event that produced it.

Hubble Discovers a Strange Warp Caused by a Giant Planet

The Cat's Tail was not the only unusual feature revealed by the new observations.

Using Hubble in a different observational configuration, Avsar and his colleagues also identified an unexpected distortion in the broad halo of dust surrounding Beta Pictoris.

The researchers suspect this strange warp may be caused by the gravitational influence of Beta Pic b, one of three planets in the system.

Beta Pic b is a massive gas giant estimated to be about 10 times the mass of Jupiter. Its powerful gravity may be disturbing the surrounding debris, altering the paths of dust particles, comets, and other icy objects across enormous distances.

"This gives us another line of evidence into how giant planets influence comets through their immense gravitational force," Avsar said. "It's a testament of how much these massive planets really influence their surrounding dust and icy bodies out to hundreds of astronomical units."

The finding highlights how giant planets can shape their environments far beyond their immediate orbits.

A Glimpse Into Our Solar System's Violent Past

For researchers, Beta Pictoris offers more than an opportunity to investigate an unusual cosmic structure. It may also provide a window into the early history of our own solar system.

Consider the Kuiper Belt, the distant region beyond Neptune that contains Pluto and numerous other icy bodies.

When the Kuiper Belt was only about 20 million years old, astronomers believe it was much more crowded than it is today. It may have contained hundreds of objects comparable in size to Pluto.

Over billions of years, the gravitational influence of the solar system's outer giant planets likely changed that environment dramatically. By disturbing the orbits of smaller bodies, these planets may have pushed many objects into new regions or expelled them from the solar system entirely, effectively "clearing out" much of the original population.

The strange dust tail and newly identified warp around Beta Pictoris may offer clues to similar processes unfolding in another planetary system.

By studying these distant structures, astronomers hope to better understand how violent collisions, migrating debris, and the immense gravity of giant planets helped transform the chaos of the early solar system into the planetary arrangement we see today.

#723. Producers Push for Year-End Passage of Trump-Backed Federal Film Incentive: AFM

With Trump and bipartisan lawmakers on board, industry figures at AFM are hoping for action before Washington’s January power shift — and some financiers are already betting on passage.

Few issues loom larger over the projects being assembled at this week’s American Film Market, Los Angeles’ annual gathering of the independent movie industry, than the fate of a proposed U.S. federal production incentive.

“A federal incentive would change the entire nature of our film and TV industry,” Josh Rogin, the Motion Picture Association’s senior vp of federal government affairs, said Tuesday during an AFM panel.

But for all the optimism around the proposal, its backers are also growing a tad anxious. Producers want Congress to act before the year ends, while President Trump’s endorsement and a bipartisan coalition remain tenuously in place. Related Stories Movies 'Long Long Night' Director Youm Kyu-bock on Creating Animation That Takes Kids Seriously Movies Is the Hope at AFM Real?

“I believe very strongly that we’re going to get this accomplished, and we have to get this done before the end of the year so that we can start planning projects for 2027,” said Steven Paul, chairman and CEO of SP Media Group.

Paul and SP Media president Scott Karol have worked closely with actor Jon Voight, Trump’s “special ambassador” to Hollywood, to develop proposals to revive U.S. production and win the president’s backing. Their efforts, along with backing from the MPA, have helped turn the longstanding industry wish for a federal incentive into an exceedingly rare point of agreement between Trump, left-leaning Hollywood and lawmakers in both parties.

Trump publicly backed a federal incentive in August, and in September, senators Tim Scott (R-S.C.) and Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) introduced the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act. House backers include Republicans Nathaniel Moran and Brian Jack alongside Democrats Linda Sánchez and Laura Friedman.

The proposal would provide a 20 percent credit on qualifying U.S. production wages, rising to a maximum of 30 percent with bonuses, including one for independent productions. It could supplement state incentives and would be transferable.

But the Democrats’ midterm “blue wave” has heightened the urgency for many. With the Senate targeting a Dec. 18 adjournment, advocates have roughly five weeks to secure the bill’s passage. Legislation left unfinished when the current lame-duck Congress ends would have to be reintroduced in the new Congress.

That could mean renewed debate over the credit’s cost and eligibility rules, alongside fresh bargaining over legislative priorities. And the bigger danger, say backers, is losing momentum as Washington’s attention shifts to the confrontation between Trump and incoming Democratic majorities. Many fear the president’s support could easily evaporate as both sides enter battle mode.

At an Oct. 30 campaign rally in Florida, Trump mocked Hollywood liberals for “kissing my ass” while seeking backing for the proposals.

“They want tax credits for Hollywood because Hollywood’s dying,” he told the crowd. “And I’ll probably do it. Should I do it? Probably.”

“It needs to get passed before the end of the year,” Karol said at AFM, “because who the hell knows what’s going to happen next year when the Democrats come in to take the House and the Senate, and then Trump gets upset because he’s a lame duck.”

Many also want swift passage so producers can plan their budgets and bank on the new support while industry momentum is running high at the box office, rather than face another bout of uncertainty.

“They need to know that if it gets passed in December, that any film that starts principal photography on or after Jan. 1 of 2027 will be able to qualify for this big new incentive — which will be amazing,” Karol added.

Some financiers at AFM have already begun positioning themselves for that possibility, and they’re allocating their investment dollars accordingly — in a way that is likely, despite the odds, to please both Trump and liberal Hollywood’s below-the-line workers. British producer-financier Head Gear Films has announced a U.S. operation and plans to invest $120 million in American independent film and television in its first year.

Its co-founder and CEO, Phil Hunt, sees a federal credit creating opportunities to finance U.S. productions using the same tax-credit lending model familiar in Britain and Europe.

“If it passes, a U.S. production gets cheaper to make,” Hunt said. “That’s why we’re setting up now, so we’re ready the day it lands.”

Scott Roxborough contributed to this report.

They say all good things come to those who wait… and WAIT. Well, the wait for "Robopocalypse" fans might finally be over, as Oscar winners Ron Howard and Akiva Goldsman have announced they're working on a TV adaptation.

It does seem like an eternity since news first broke that Portland-based New York Times bestselling author Daniel H. Wilson’s "Robopocalypse" (Doubleday, 2011) was bought by Steven Spielberg’s DreamWorks SKG for a sci-fi spectacle, with Drew Goddard ("The Martian") brought in to pen the screenplay.

That was back in 2009, and since then the story of a rogue AI named Archos and a hearty band of indigenous people in America’s heartland battling to save humanity from extinction has been placed on Hollywood’s back burner. After numerous stalled starts and director Michael Bay getting involved in 2018, "Robopocalypse" was quietly powered down due to script issues, filmmaker scheduling conflicts, and the enormous budget required.

But now we have been blessed with the news, first broken by The Hollywood Reporter, that Ron Howard ("Apollo 13," "The Da Vinci Code") and Akiva Goldsman ("A Beautiful Mind," "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds") have taken up the mantle of this chilling sci-fi project to develop as a new TV series. And what timing, just as AI fever has gripped the planet with paranoia centered around our eventual robot overlords.

"'Robopocalypse' has all the scale and suspense of a major action story, but what drew me to it are the thought-provoking themes and humanity at its center," Ron Howard shared in a statement.

The cover of 2011's smash sci-fi hit Robopocalypse by Daniel H. Wilson

The cover of the 2014 sequel Robogenesis by Daniel H. Wilson

"Daniel created a future that feels both startling and increasingly plausible, with characters who must figure out what connects us when the technology we rely on turns against us. I am also thrilled to work with Akiva again. We have shared some incredibly meaningful creative experiences, and this feels like the right story to bring us back together."

As a PhD graduate of Carnegie Mellon University’s Robotics Institute and a future king of the techno-thriller, Wilson was the ideal writer to bring this frightening story to life, and a 2014 sequel titled "Robogenesis" was equally gripping.

The prolific, award-winning writer has since set up a multitude of other Hollywood projects spawned from his catalog of works, including "Amped," "The Clockwork Dynasty," the authorized sequel to Michael Crichton's "The Andromeda Strain," "The Andromeda Evolution," and his 2025 alien invasion novel "Hole in the Sky," still alive at Netflix.

Howard's Imagine Entertainment will partner with Akiva Goldsman's Weed Road Pictures on this episodic adaptation, with Howard attached to direct the pilot episode and Goldsman serving as series showrunner.

"Robopocalypse" marks a creative reunion for the distinguished creators, following their collaborations on "A Beautiful Mind," "Cinderella Man," "The Da Vinci Code," and "Angels & Demons." Spielberg's Amblin Entertainment is slated to executive produce the ambitious show alongside Imagine's Brian Grazer and Jeb Brody and Weed's Rachel Wizenberg and Greg Lessans.

It's too early to tell which streaming service the "Robopocalypse" TV show will be attached to yet. Hopefully the pilot episode wows one of the big names, and we can finally see the "Robopocalypse" adaptation of our dreams.

In the meantime, we'd recommend checking out the original book by Daniel H. Wilson.

Not far into our future, the dazzling technology that runs our world turns against us. Controlled by a childlike—yet massively powerful—artificial intelligence known as Archos, the global network of machines on which our world has grown dependent suddenly becomes an implacable, deadly foe.

Jeff Spry is an award-winning screenwriter and veteran freelance journalist covering TV, movies, video games, books, and comics. His work has appeared at SYFY Wire, Inverse, Collider, Bleeding Cool and elsewhere. Jeff lives in beautiful Bend, Oregon amid the ponderosa pines, classic muscle cars, a crypt of collector horror comics, and two loyal English Setters.

#720. ‘Exotic’ Takes Us to Polish Pole Dance Camp to Tell a Female Story of Self-Discovery and Body Confidence

Writer-director Sonja Orlewicz-Zakrzewska shot her debut feature, premiering at Tallinn, during the Exo Stars Camp, among real participants and instructors.

If you have been longing for a feature film about pole-dancing Poles, Exotic (Eksootika) is just what you were looking for! If you want to see a movie about self-discovery, body confidence, being exactly who you are and living life without asking permission, Exotic is also for you. Interested in a story about female friendship and belonging? Again, Exotic has got you covered. But even if you feel you would never care to catch a film about a writer’s attempt to master exotic pole dancing in a Polish beach resort, Exotic may well surprise you.

The feature debut of writer-director Sonja Orlewicz-Zakrzewska, who is also a visual artist and photographer, is full of humor, self-doubt and vulnerability. Adding authenticity, Exotic was shot during a recent edition of the Exo Stars Camp, a pole-dancing camp in a Polish beach town, and includes real participants and instructors. Related Stories Movies 'Long Long Night' Director Youm Kyu-bock on Creating Animation That Takes Kids Seriously Movies Brandon Sklenar on 'Iron Jane,' Body Dysmorphia and His Rapid Hollywood Rise

The film will have its world premiere in the First Feature Competition of the 30th edition of the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival (PÖFF) on Saturday, Nov. 14.

The filmmaker attended the camp herself and felt there was a story to tell. “I was fascinated by the clash of the fragile, intimate universes we carried within us around the camp,” she says. “It soon became clear that the camp itself was a perfect place to confront fears, leave one’s comfort zone and express oneself more than daily life ever allows.”

Exotic reflects that journey. It follows Mila, who is 30 and insecure. When her friend cancels on her, she reluctantly travels to a pole-dancing camp on the Polish coast alone, where she finds herself surrounded by confident dancers, skimpy costumes, high heels and a world that feels alien. But away from everyday life at home, her initial irony and unease give way to a journey of self-discovery.

Or as the PÖFF website teases: “Through demanding training, wild nights, awkward encounters, laughter, and intimate conversations, she discovers freedom, friendship, and a new relationship with herself.”

Mozaika Films is the main production company behind Exotic. The producers are Magdalena Sztorc and Anna Zajaczkowska. The cast is led by Jasmina Polak. The cinematographer was Adam Suzin, with editing handled by Tomasz Kajetan Naruszewicz. Pluto Film is handling sales.

Orlewicz-Zakrzewska talked to THR about mixing real-life experiences with fiction, how she made sure that her protagonist’s journey felt so believable and why pole dancing deserves a much better rep.

In case you don’t believe that real life inspired Exotic, just listen to the filmmaker. “I’m a pole dancer. I’ve been pole dancing for four years now,” she tells THR. “The main character in the film is played by Jasmina Polak. She’s actually a very good friend of mine in private life, and we went to pole-dancing classes together. After one or two months, we found out about the camp and decided to go together. But it was Jasmina who canceled at the last moment.”

So, Orlewicz-Zakrzewska attended the camp on her own. “Not everything in a film, but a lot of things you see are actually very much like my own experience and story,” she shares. “I did actually have those two roommates you see in the film, who were both kind of crazy in a different way. So, a lot of things there are inspired by reality.”

Orlewicz-Zakrzewska says she “fell in love with pole dancing right away.” And yes, she is aware that there still is a stigma attached to it. “There is a lot of it, and that’s why the pole-dancing community, all my girls, are really amazed by the fact that we shot this film,” she tells THR. “I did research about that and actually found out that it’s actually the first film that shows pole dance as a sport. There is no other full-length feature that shows the pole-dancing community as a sports community, as a hobby community rather than in a context of strip clubs.”

What does she love about it? “There are so many things,” Orlewicz-Zakrzewska says. “First, it’s an amazing workout. Your core strength is insane. For me, the gym is so boring. I also really like the femininity in this dance. And the more strength you have, the more effortless and, in a sense, more feminine and graceful you look. And then in your mind, the strength links up with the feminine.”

Exotic also shows the fun and party aspects that can come with the workouts. “I really love the fact that it has this entourage” and community spirit, explains Orlewicz-Zakrzewska. “The reason why I never explored it [before she started pole dancing] was that I was scared of judgment. I was scared of the patriarchal eye. There is a certain judgmental eye towards the pole-dancing community.”

How about the skimpy outfits? “You do often wear almost nothing, which actually makes a lot of sense because of the sweat and because you need your skin to hold on,” the filmmaker explains. “And the high-heeled shoes actually make a lot of sense when doing the spins [or jumps].”

And wearing these outfits and pole dancing opened her up to accepting a side of her that she was not willing to even consider before. “I have never been a girly girl,” shares Orlewicz-Zakrzewska. “I have always been a little bit intellectual and ran around with boys and climbed trees and so on. But I always had this other side in me, and [pole-dancing allowed me to] explore this more open form of femininity.”

Showcasing pole dancing and its community is something that excited the filmmaker and the folks at the camp. The writer-director actually knew right away that she would return to the post-Soviet hotel, where the camp takes place, with the camera. And she did.

But how did she approach the shoot and getting the people at the camp involved? “Before it started, I told the participants [and instructors] that I wanted to shoot the film. Is everybody okay with that? If anybody’s not, just please say no,” Orlewicz-Zakrzewska recalls saying. “And imagine: nobody said no. Not a single person! Because they are performers, and most people in pole dancing are really open. So, they were really happy that we were doing this film and showing this community the way it really is.”

So keep your eyes open for non-professional actors in Exotic! “All is scripted, but we were just putting our actresses and actors inside the actual situations, inside the actual classes,” the director explains.

Exotic also features a 2007 clip of Jonas Mekas, the late Lithuanian filmmaker and poet who has been called “the godfather of American avant-garde cinema,” defending Paris Hilton. He argued that society has become too negative and skeptical to believe that people can actually change.

Which gets us to the question of Mila’s change in Exotic. Her transformation is neither instantaneous nor dramatic, and that is by design. The filmmaker recalls her experience at Exo Stars Campo. “It’s just really, really intense, you are outside of your everyday social bubble and you really have to confront the question of how you want to be perceived by others,” Orlewicz-Zakrzewska tells THR. “It’s about both your relationship with yourself and also your relationship with the people you meet. So there are mechanisms that help you grow internally and reflect. But at the same time, nothing really happens because it’s just a sports camp. There are limitations to the massiveness of the internal journey.”

Her conclusion: “It’s not that a real revolution is going to happen there. But there is maybe the seed of the revolution that you are going to carry on with you.”

Exotic is Orlewicz-Zakrzewska’s first feature film, but it wasn’t supposed to be. “I was actually working on two other big projects before, but this one happened to get finished first,” she tells THR, adding with a laugh. “Maybe the reason why Exotic was produced as the first one is that it’s the most ‘normal’ thing I ever wrote. All the other things are much crazier.”

So, what’s next for her? “I’m working on two other feature films and a series,” Orlewicz-Zakrzewska says. “But all of these things are in development.”

It will be interesting to see if her next project has a short title, just like Exotic, or a really long one. After all, the title of her debut feature went through an evolution. “What’s funny is that with the titles for the things I write, it’s always either a full, super-long sentence or just one word. It’s never in between,” Orlewicz-Zakrzewska explains. And she shares the first title she had for Exotic, and it is indeed long: If the World Is Round, I Don’t Know What It Means to Be Ahead.

#719. Hidden climate superpower: Why some ocean “snow” carries six times more carbon

Far below the ocean's surface, a constant snowfall drifts through the darkness. But unlike the frozen flakes that fall from the sky, this underwater snow consists of tiny clumps of waste, dead organisms, and other debris. Known as marine snow, these particles contain everything from mucus and animal feces to silt and the remains of microscopic plankton.

As this material sinks, it carries enormous quantities of carbon from the upper ocean toward the seafloor. Researchers estimate that marine snow removes more than 10 gigatons of carbon from surface waters each year. Yet only about two gigatons reach depths where that carbon can remain stored for hundreds or even thousands of years.

Why so much carbon fails to make it into the deep ocean has long puzzled scientists. Now, researchers from UC San Diego's Scripps Institution of Oceanography and the University of Lincoln have identified a surprisingly important factor: how sticky the marine snow is.

Their findings, published October 8 in the journal Science, show that the viscosity, or thickness and gooeyness, of marine snow influences how quickly bacteria break it apart and how far it can sink. According to the researchers, the stickiest particles can transport more than six times as much carbon to the deep ocean as particles with a thinner, less viscous consistency.

Marine snow plays an important role in Earth's carbon cycle, the natural movement of carbon among the atmosphere, oceans, land, and living organisms. By transporting carbon into deep water, sinking particles can keep some of it isolated from the atmosphere for centuries or longer.

However, not every particle survives the journey. Bacteria feed on marine snow as it descends, gradually breaking down the material and affecting how much carbon reaches the ocean's depths.

The new research provides the first detailed look at how living bacteria interact with the physical structure of marine snow and, more broadly, mucus itself. These interactions are important well beyond the ocean's carbon cycle. Similar relationships between bacteria and mucus help sustain coral reefs, kelp forests, plant root systems, and the digestive systems of humans and other animals.

Until recently, scientists lacked the technology to observe these interactions at the microscopic scale needed to understand them.

A Four-Year Quest to See Inside Marine Snow

The project began in 2021, when Bryce Inman, then a postdoctoral researcher at Scripps Oceanography, set out to explore what he calls "the muscoscape."

"Observing individual bacteria interacting with the physical structure of mucus had never been possible," said Inman.

Together with colleagues including Farooq Azam, a microbiologist and professor emeritus at Scripps, Inman spent four years trying to overcome that limitation. Multiple attempts were unsuccessful before the team finally developed a working technique in 2025.

Their solution combined 3D confocal microscopy with specially designed fluorescent molecules. Confocal microscopy uses light to capture detailed images at different depths within a sample, allowing researchers to reconstruct its structure in three dimensions. The fluorescent molecules helped make features of the material visible.

For the first time, the scientists could examine the "physical terrain" of individual marine snow particles while watching how living bacteria moved through and interacted with them.

The images revealed a surprisingly intricate microscopic environment, complete with structural differences that affect where bacteria can settle and how easily they can reach the material inside.

Much like snowflakes in the atmosphere, marine snow particles vary considerably. Each contains its own mixture of organic and inorganic materials, creating differences in composition, structure, and viscosity.

The researchers' new imaging approach, described in a companion study published in Nature Communications, revealed that bacteria preferentially colonize areas near a particle's surface where the material is less viscous.

The denser, stickier regions deeper inside are much harder for bacteria to penetrate.

"Bacteria can latch on to less viscous portions of each particle, but cannot reach more viscous regions until they break it down," said Inman. "Think of it like a worm in an apple: the flesh is easy to penetrate, but the core is tough to chew through"

This difference has important consequences for how long marine snow remains intact.

In laboratory experiments, the scientists observed that particles with greater viscosity resisted bacterial degradation and fragmentation for longer periods. Computer simulations further suggested that these stickier particles can descend to greater depths before breaking apart.

Based on these results, the team estimates that highly viscous marine snow can deliver more than six times as much carbon to the deep ocean as less viscous particles.

The findings help explain why some sinking material transports carbon much farther into the ocean than other particles, even though both begin their journeys near the surface.

"How far marine snow can sink is a surprisingly complicated problem, and we have added another - very gooey - piece to the puzzle," said Inman.

A Discovery With Implications Beyond the Ocean

Although the research focuses on marine snow, its implications extend to many environments where bacteria interact with mucus.

Mucus is often regarded as a relatively simple, slippery substance. But the new imaging technology reveals that it has a complex internal landscape, with microscopic structures that can influence how bacteria behave.

Understanding these physical features could help scientists investigate biological processes in settings ranging from human digestive health to the recovery of damaged coral reefs.

The method also opens opportunities to explore interactions that previously could not be observed directly, providing researchers with a new way to study the microscopic environments inhabited by bacteria.

Mucus, slime, whatever you want to call it, "has a surprising amount of structure," Inman said. "There are bulges, crevasses, all this sort of structure to it that we really had no idea about at a scale smaller than bacteria. This is the first time we're really examining this physical habitat."

The discovery adds an important missing piece to scientists' understanding of how carbon travels through the ocean. It also demonstrates that something as seemingly ordinary as the thickness of underwater slime can have far-reaching consequences for the planet's natural systems.

Additional funding for the research was provided by the Simons Foundation and the Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council.

"The door was open on this theory — that Little Red Dots could be primordial black holes. We've now cracked it open a little farther."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Ever since NASA's James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) started observing the early universe, it has been providing almost as many surprises as it has answers. One such surprise are the so-called Little Red Dots, cosmic objects that seemingly disappear completely before the universe is two billion years old.

New research suggests that Little Red Dots may actually be connected primordial black holes, tiny black holes born not from dying stars but rather from fluctuations in the density of matter just after the Big Bang, in the earliest moments of cosmic history. Should they exist, primordial black holes would predate stars, galactic dust particles, and elements heavier than hydrogen and helium. Now, researchers have used JWST data to test whether one particular Little Red Dot, known as blackAbell 2744-QSO1 (QSO1), could host a primordial black hole.

"A black hole is an object born from the gravitational death of a star. Primordial black holes are a very different story," study team member Valerio De Luca, of the Department of Physics and Astronomy at Johns Hopkins University (JHU) in Maryland, said in a statement.

"They come from the physics of the early universe that predates the first stars, when the universe was expanding exponentially in time and space. So the mechanisms for creating primordial black holes are different," De Luca added.

Though scientists have theorized about the existence of primordial black holes since they were first proposed by Stephen Hawking in the 1970s, no hard evidence has presented itself. One of the issues scientists have puzzled over is how to tell the difference between a primordial black hole and a "traditional" or astrophysical black hole formed from the supernova death and collapse of a massive star.

"Little Red Dots could surround astrophysical black holes, and most probably many of them do, but they could also be primordial black holes, if primordial black holes exist," De Luca said. "So the question becomes, Which ones are primordial and how can we tell?"

De Luca and colleagues turned their attention to QS01, located around 13.1 billion light-years from Earth, which is seen as it was just 700 million years after the Big Bang. What makes this Little Red Dot stand out is the fact that it is almost entirely composed of hydrogen and helium. Because these were the universe's first elements, it could be more unspoiled and primordial than other Little Red Dots.

The team modeled how a Little Red Dot like QS01 could form from a primordial black hole. That was necessary because the circumstances under which this could happen would have to be very specific.

"There are constraints on primordial black holes from cosmological observations," said team member Loris Del Grosso, also of JHU's Department of Physics and Astronomy. "There can only be so many primordial black holes in the universe, for example, and there cannot be too many of them in a given cluster."

Considering three possible scenarios, the team found that the most likely situation is a smaller primordial black hole consuming surrounding gas and energy until it grew to be the size of QSO1.

"The door was open on this theory — that Little Red Dots could be primordial black holes," Del Grosso said. "We've now cracked it open a little farther by showing some scenarios are more likely than others."

Del Grosso and crew now intend to look at the other 100 or so Little Red Dots seen by the JWST to determine how many of them could have started life as primordial black holes.

Then scientists may finally have the evidence to say these long-theorized ancient black holes actually existed.

"We don't have a clear understanding of what happens in the early universe right after the Big Bang," De Luca concluded. "If primordial black holes do exist, then something had to happen to make them in the first place, which would be a groundbreaking discovery in physics."

The team's findings were published in June in the journal Physical Review Letters.

#717. Biotech innovations are an opportunity to limit climate change

Climate change is affecting many types of crop, including these unusually small potatoes.Credit: John Thys/AFP/Getty

Policymakers at the United Nations COP31 climate conference that started this week in Antalya, Turkey, will know that the UN Environment Programme has confirmed that global warming will exceed the limit of 1.5 °C above pre-industrial temperatures agreed in 2015 in Paris. This meeting comes hot on the heels of the UN COP17 biodiversity summit in Yerevan, Armenia, which affirmed yet again that the world is also in the middle of a biodiversity crisis. Progress in each case, whether preventing dangerous climate change or stemming biodiversity loss, is too slow. But researchers across scientific disciplines are now arguing that advances in biotechnology could provide solutions1. Methods such as gene editing and germplasm mining — the analysis of huge libraries of plant-genome sequences to find useful traits for crop improvement — can now be used to tackle global warming and protect nature, scientists write in a climate-themed issue of Nature Biotechnology.

There was a time — not that long ago — when many considered biotechnologies a threat to the environment. But as the special issue shows, a shift is under way. Now, the field offers strategies for protecting both climate and biodiversity from the many damaging effects of industrial agriculture.

To feed a growing global population, between 2015 and 2024, the amount of cultivated land grew by roughly eight million hectares a year1. Yet, if the greenhouse-gas emissions, and thus global warming, this expansion causes is to be avoided, the world must work out how to produce enough food within its current agricultural footprint. Land clearance and land-use change contributes up to five billion tonnes of carbon annually — and is a major cause of biodiversity loss. Here, biotech solutions have some of the greatest potential, for example, by helping to increase crop yields and to protect plants from heat, drought and disease.

How biotechnology can mitigate climate change by curbing the global land squeeze

How biotechnology can mitigate climate change by curbing the global land squeeze

Of 77 such technologies with applications in agriculture, aquaculture and other sectors, many are ready for large-scale testing in the field, propose bioengineers Shekhar Mishra, Lauren Lui and Adam Arkin at the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory in California in a Perspective article2. Argentina, China and the United States have given the green light to engineered drought-tolerant crops.

Rice farming produces around 9% of human-caused emissions of the greenhouse gas methane. Now, researchers have found a way to slash these emissions, write agronomist Yunkai Jin at Hunan Agricultural University in Changsha, China, and his colleagues in a Comment article3.

But technological readiness isn’t enough: governments, regulators and the public need to be ready, too4. Readers might have a sense of déjà vu: in the 1990s, advances in biotechnology promised a revolution in food and agriculture — which subsequently stalled. The ambition was to genetically modify crops or engineer them in other ways so that they could tolerate herbicides, resist insects and fight viruses. But, at the time, many scientists, governments and corporations promoting the technology gave insufficient attention to several issues.

Deployability of biotechnologies for environmentally resilient agriculture

Deployability of biotechnologies for environmentally resilient agriculture

One concern was public anxiety about the idea of eating food produced using transgenic technologies — crops modified by inserting a gene from another plant species or other organism. Another issue was that risks to the environment and to human health had not been studied sufficiently. A third problem was that multinational companies dominated both the research and the development of these technologies, creating fears that the rise of agricultural biotechnology would put many small family farms out of business.

Environmental groups found common cause with consumer organizations. Together, they urged governments to enact strict regulations. In the European Union, for example, risks to human health and the environment needed to be assessed before technologies producing genetically modified organisms could be commercialized. Although this was necessary, it slowed down advances in low- and middle-income countries, because any nation intending to export produce to the EU would have to prove that it was not genetically modified.

Since then, at least two things have changed, increasing optimism about the use of biotechnology to help the planet. The discovery of gene editing — in which an organism’s genes are modified precisely to produce specific traits — has proved transformational for agriculture. The method is being developed cautiously and is regulated in a more nuanced way than were conventional technologies that produce genetically modified crops. In June, the EU amended its regulations on genetic modification and now permits the cultivation of some gene-edited crops.

Low-methane rice is near — the world should deploy it

Low-methane rice is near — the world should deploy it

A second development is that catastrophic events such as heatwaves and floods have meant that climate change and the planet’s protection have become mainstream concerns across science and society, not just for environmental research. In a way, we all need to be environmentalists now, and this provides a rationale for governments to reconsider adopting biotech solutions with appropriate safeguards in place.

Advances in biotechnology that limit land use should be deployed to slow down the rise in global temperatures and biodiversity loss. This will require a partnership between the private sector, scientists, conservationists and farmers. High-yielding crops produced using industrial agriculture have helped to feed the world but have also had a devastating effect on biodiversity. Organic agriculture is more sustainable but requires extra land, because its yields tend to be lower than those from industrial methods. Providing they are implemented wisely, safely and ethically, biotechnologies could contribute to innovative farming methods that offer the best of both worlds.
